entries.label: Justice's path through the work
entries.summary: The argument is the search after justice: hinted at by Cephalus, argued on proverbial morality by Socrates and Polemarchus, caricatured by Thrasymachus and partly answered, then abstracted by Glaucon and Adeimantus until justice, invisible in the individual, reappears in the ideal State. From there the treatment moves through education, the higher State ruled by philosopher-kings, the decline through honour-loving government, democracy and tyranny, the resumed quarrel with poetry (poetry as imitation thrice removed from truth, Homer banished), and finally a revelation of a future life.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · the introduction's commentator

entries.label: Fivefold structure; opposed halves
entries.summary: The division into books is judged later than Plato; five natural divisions are proposed (introductory refutation of popular justice; construction of the first State and education; Books V–VII, where philosophy and a communist State ruled by philosophers replace justice as the question; the decline of States and of men; the conclusion on poetry and the afterlife). A broader split into Books I–IV (Hellenic religion and morality) and V–X (an ideal kingdom of philosophy) yields two really opposed points of view, making the Republic an imperfect whole; whether this reflects an enlarged plan, unresolved conflicting ideas, or composition at different times cannot be settled.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · the introduction's commentator

entries.label: Against a single design
entries.summary: The commentator warns that too much is made of referring every work to a single design: plans grow under an author's hand, and one may as well speak of many designs as one. On this reading the State is a vehicle for several great truths (the idea of good as divine perfection, justice as human perfection, lifelong education, false teachers and evil rulers, a kingdom laid up in heaven), freely mixing ideas, myths, figures and facts; its practicability is therefore irrelevant to its truth. Still, justice is said to bear greater marks of design than the State's framework, and Books V–VII the summit of speculation.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · the introduction's commentator

entries.label: Characters as moral stages
entries.summary: Plato's interlocutors are said to represent successive stages of morality: the old Athenian gentleman Cephalus (who raises justice while resting secure in honest dealing) gives way to the proverbial morality of Polemarchus, then the Sophists' wild generalization in Thrasymachus (Plato's caricature of a celebrated man), and finally the young disciples Glaucon and Adeimantus. These last are distinct rather than doubled roles: Glaucon is vivid, humorous and imaginative and takes the lighter passages, Adeimantus graver and more argumentative, holding Socrates to explanations of women and children, happiness, and the corruption of philosophy.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · the introduction's commentator

entries.label: Socrates' shifting portrayal
entries.summary: The delineation of Socrates is called not wholly consistent: Book I shows the ironical, questioning opponent of the Sophists known from Xenophon and the Apology, whereas later his hostility to the Sophists abates and he grows dogmatic and constructive, passing beyond the political or speculative range of the historical Socrates. The Socratic method is retained in form but has become a method of teaching through interlocutors who look at a thesis from several points of view.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · the introduction's commentator

entries.label: First definitions of justice fail
entries.summary: The commentator presents Cephalus' 'tell the truth and pay your debts' and Polemarchus' Simonidean 'do good to friends and harm to enemies' as two aphoristic definitions broken by counterexamples (the madman's sword; the impossibility that justice should make men worse), leaving two unconnected precepts without a common principle.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates, Cephalus, Polemarchus (reported in the editor's analysis)

entries.label: Thrasymachus: might is right
entries.summary: Thrasymachus (as reported) answers that justice is the interest of the stronger — rulers make laws for their own interest — and adds that injustice is more profitable and stronger than justice; Cleitophon's variant makes justice what the ruler thinks his interest to be.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Thrasymachus (reported in the editor's analysis)

entries.label: Book I ends in aporia
entries.summary: Socrates closes the festival discussion confessing that he still does not know what justice is and so cannot judge whether the just are happier; the editor adds that Thrasymachus' fabric is demolished but nothing is concluded, Socrates resuming the 'know-nothing' stance.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates (reported in the editor's analysis)

entries.label: Art-virtue analogy is era-bound
entries.summary: Editorial commentary argues that the analogy of arts and virtues reflects an age when art, virtue, and the moral and intellectual faculties were not yet distinguished (Aristotle's art/virtue distinction being later), though the absurd result 'justice is a thief' and Socrates' dissatisfaction hint that virtue is more than art; the 'art of pay' and the phrasing about the injured being made worse are called verbal flaws.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · editorial commentator

entries.label: Glaucon reopens: justice in itself
entries.summary: Glaucon rejects Socrates' indirect ending of Book I, sorts goods into three classes and moves justice to the disputed middle class; he and Adeimantus demand that justice be commended in itself, by its power in the soul, with reputation excluded — the just man being thought unjust and the unjust just.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Glaucon and Adeimantus (reported in the editor's analysis)

entries.label: Ideal happiness and caveats
entries.summary: Commentary says the two brothers ask Socrates to prove the just happy once everything ordinarily counted as happiness is taken away. It defends such an attempt: every ideal is paradoxical beside ordinary conditions of life and is rarely realized, though a few exceptional individuals may have happiness in death and misery. It adds that Plato is dramatizing one aspect of ethical truth in a series of positions rather than stating his own final conclusion, and that 'happiness' should not be read as the modern notion of conscious pleasure or satisfaction.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Justice enlarged to social order
entries.summary: Commentary reports Adeimantus, taking up Glaucon's hint, arguing that mankind values justice only for rewards and reputation — the advantage convention gives to Thrasymachus and Glaucon — while both brothers question whether morality turns on consequences and go past Socrates' position that justice is desirable both for itself and its results. Commentary then proposes that Socrates enlarges the old-fashioned notion of justice into universal order or well-being, first in the State and then the individual, as the ordering principle of the other three virtues, while trying to reconcile an internal account of justice with man's being a social creature.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Justice as own-work order
entries.summary: The analysis reports Socrates treating the perfect city as containing wisdom, courage, temperance and justice and finding justice as the remainder once the other three are eliminated. Temperance is figured as a harmony in which the better rules the worse and the classes are attuned like strings; justice is then found in the old division of labour — each person and each class doing his own business, with grave evil when one person combines the offices of trainer, warrior and legislator. The definition is declared provisional until tested in the individual.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates (reported in the analysis)

entries.label: Justice and temperance blur
entries.summary: The commentator objects that ideas cannot be separated like chemical substances: the Republic's definitions of justice and temperance are hard to tell apart, since temperance is a harmony of discordant elements and justice the perfect order in which all natures and classes do their own business — so they differ in degree rather than kind. The justice-and-temperance definitions are said to reappear from a provisional definition in the Charmides (162 A), and the omission of temperance is called a trick of style.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Adeimantus on shifting terms
entries.summary: Adeimantus objects to the form of the Socratic reasoning (the elenchus extracts answers by the way questions are put), and the commentator notes that long arguments let words drift in meaning unbeknownst, so verbal argumentations cannot match the precision of numerical symbols.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Adeimantus (objection as reported); introduction's author

entries.label: Old age: temper, not years
entries.summary: Cephalus reports that complaints of old age misattribute their cause: the burdens of age fall on men of ungoverned temper, while a calm nature feels little pressure; he cites Sophocles on escaping a mad master of passion.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Cephalus (narrated by Socrates)

entries.label: Wealth and deathbed conscience
entries.summary: Prodded by Socrates' suggestion that wealth, not disposition, makes age bearable, Cephalus answers that riches' greatest benefit to a good man is enabling him to avoid wronging others and to face death without fear of unpaid debts or divine penalties—something neither virtue alone nor riches alone secures.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Cephalus (narrated by Socrates)

entries.label: Justice: good to friends, harm to enemies
entries.summary: After Socrates defeats the formula 'speak truth and pay debts' with the case of a weapon lent to a friend gone mad, Polemarchus inherits the argument and, via Simonides, first says justice is repaying debts, then that it is giving what is proper to each—construed as doing good to friends and evil to enemies, later corrected to those who are really (not merely seemingly) good or bad.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Polemarchus (on Simonides; questioned by Socrates)

entries.label: The just cannot injure anyone
entries.summary: Socrates argues that injuring a person worsens him in human virtue, i.e. makes him unjust, and that no art or good produces its own opposite—so harming even a bad enemy cannot be an act of justice, refuting the debt-repayment formula and prompting Polemarchus's agreement.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Socrates (with Polemarchus assenting)

entries.label: Justice is the interest of the stronger
entries.summary: Abandoning the preceding exchange as folly, Thrasymachus proclaims that justice is nothing other than the interest of the stronger: each regime makes laws for its own advantage and calls obedience to them justice, so universally justice is the interest of the government.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Thrasymachus (narrated by Socrates)

entries.label: Fallible rulers contradict that claim
entries.summary: Socrates objects that rulers can legislate contrary to their own interest; since subjects must obey, justice on Thrasymachus's showing becomes the injury of the stronger as much as his interest—a conclusion clearest in Socrates' own restatement and granted by Polemarchus.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Socrates (Polemarchus concurring)

entries.label: Cleitophon: what rulers think useful
entries.summary: Cleitophon intervenes with a salvage reading: Thrasymachus meant the interest the stronger merely thinks to be his interest—though Polemarchus denies these were Thrasymachus's words, and Thrasymachus himself rejects the amendment, refusing to call the mistaken a ruler at that moment.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Cleitophon (disputed by Polemarchus and Thrasymachus)

entries.label: No craft erring in respect of itself
entries.summary: Thrasymachus's second line of defence, preserved here chiefly in an editorial sidenote, is that no artist or ruler errs in so far as he really is what his name implies; his own quoted words deny that one who is mistaken counts as 'stronger' at that moment. The full reply continues beyond the core text supplied.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Thrasymachus (reply partly preserved in an editorial sidenote)

entries.label: Justice = stronger's interest
entries.summary: In dialogue, Thrasymachus defends 'justice is the interest of the stronger' by a qua-principle: no craftsman, sage, or ruler errs insofar as he is what his name implies (earlier talk of erring practitioners was loose speech), so the ruler qua ruler commands what is for his own interest and the subject must obey.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Thrasymachus, replying to Socrates

entries.label: Arts serve their subjects
entries.summary: Socrates argues that an art has no defect of its own to correct and therefore considers only the interest of its subject-matter (medicine serves the body, horsemanship the horse); ruling arts (physician, pilot) therefore prescribe for the subject's good, not the ruler's profit. Thrasymachus gives reluctant assents, reported in the dialogue.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Socrates, with Thrasymachus's reluctant assents

entries.label: Justice is another's good
entries.summary: Thrasymachus retorts that shepherds and state rulers study their own advantage: justice is in reality another's good, the ruler's interest and the subject's loss, while injustice is one's own profit. He instances partnerships, taxation, office, and above all tyranny, where wholesale fraud and force win happiness and praise.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Thrasymachus, in his sustained speech

entries.label: Art of payment distinguished
entries.summary: Socrates distinguishes each art's proper function (medicine gives health, navigation safety) from the separate art of payment; a practitioner's gain comes from an added use of the paid art, not from the art he professes, and he benefits his subject even when unpaid.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Socrates, with Thrasymachus's reluc

entries.label: Injustice as virtue and wisdom
entries.summary: Socrates expresses amazement that Thrasymachus classes injustice with wisdom and virtue and justice with folly; Thrasymachus explicitly confirms the classification ('Certainly I do so class them'; 'You have guessed most infallibly'), so the dispute is no longer on received principles.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Socrates characterizing; Thrasymachus confirming

entries.label: Knower does not exceed his like
entries.summary: Socrates generalizes that a knowledgeable person would claim the same as his like rather than more, while the ignorant desire more than both, and derives that the just (who claims more only of the unjust) resembles the wise and good and the unjust the ignorant — granted repeatedly but with extreme reluctance by Thrasymachus.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Socrates, with Thrasymachus's reluctant admissions

entries.label: Injustice defeats common action
entries.summary: Socrates argues injustice creates discord and is self-frustrating wherever it dwells: no city, army, family, or even a single person can act in common while unjust, so even successful evil-doers must retain some justice to cooperate. Thrasymachus agrees, at one point declining to oppose the speaker for fear of displeasing the company — a qualification preserved in the dialogue.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Socrates, with Thrasymachus's qualified agreements

entries.label: Justice as soul's excellence
entries.summary: The exchange presumes, with agreement, that justice is the excellence of the soul and injustice its defect.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Socrates (questioner) and Thrasymachus (respondent)

entries.label: Justice leads to happiness
entries.summary: Argued chain: the just soul and just person live well; to live well is to be blessed and happy; hence the just are happy and the unjust miserable — a claim met with agreement in each step.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Socrates (questioner) with Thrasymachus' assent

entries.label: Injustice never more profitable
entries.summary: From the claims that happiness, not misery, is profitable, the inference is drawn and addressed to Thrasymachus that injustice can never be more profitable than justice.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Socrates to Thrasymachus

entries.label: Thrasymachus concedes the close
entries.summary: Thrasymachus twice closes the exchange, first with 'So be it' and then offering the argument to Socrates as 'entertainment at the Bendidea'.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Thrasymachus

entries.label: Editor: Socrates displeased
entries.summary: An editor's sidenote characterizes Socrates as displeased with himself and with the argument.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · commentary · Unnamed editor/annotator (sidenote)

entries.label: Aporia: justice never defined
entries.summary: Socrates, speaking for himself, faults his own procedure of moving between questions and concludes he knows nothing: without knowing what justice is he cannot know whether it is virtue and wisdom or folly, nor whether the just are happy.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Glaucon revives the challenge
entries.summary: Glaucon, dissatisfied with Thrasymachus's retirement, asks Socrates whether he really persuades that justice always beats injustice, then announces a three-part case: the conventional origin of justice; that it is practised unwillingly and of necessity; and that (against his own view) the reputed argument makes the unjust life out to be better. He asks to hear justice praised in respect of itself.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Glaucon (asked of Socrates; narrated by Socrates)

entries.label: Three classes of goods
entries.summary: Glaucon distinguishes goods prized only for their own sake, goods prized both intrinsically and for results (knowledge, sight, health), and goods only for their results though disagreeable. Socrates places justice in the highest class, against the many who count it in the troublesome, rewarded class.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Glaucon proposes; Socrates assents and classifies

entries.label: Justice as compact of the weak
entries.summary: Reporting the common view, Glaucon says doing injustice is naturally good and suffering it evil; unable to secure the one without the other, men covenant not to do or suffer it, so that legal-and-just is a tolerated middle state, honoured only because men lack power to be unjust.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Glaucon reporting 'they say'

entries.label: Ring of Gyges: justice of necessity
entries.summary: Glaucon's ring tale (Gyges seizes an invisibility ring, seduces the queen, kills the king) is used to argue that no one stands fast in justice given safe impunity: just and unjust alike follow interest and reach the same acts, so men are just only of necessity and from incapacity.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Glaucon (traditional tale of Gyges)

entries.label: Stripped portraits of the two lives
entries.summary: Glaucon constructs two ideal types: a perfectly unjust man who is never unjust or found out and keeps the greatest reputation for justice and all its advantages, and a wholly just man who 'wishes to be and not to seem good', is credited with injustice and dies unbenefited; on these extremes judgment of the happier life is to be given.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Glaucon

entries.label: Adeimantus: praise is for outcomes
entries.summary: Adeimantus adds that parents, poets (Hesiod, Homer, Musaeus), and prose writers praise justice only for reputation, office, divine gifts and afterlife drink, blame injustice with hell-pains, call vice easy and virtue toilsome, and let sins be expiated by sacrifices and mysteries so the gods can be persuaded. The young then rationally conclude, with Pindar, to combine injustice with the appearance of justice.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Adeimantus (quoting poets and common opinion)

entries.label: Praise justice in the soul itself
entries.summary: Adeimantus charges that no panegyrist has shown justice's and injustice's essential nature in the soul, justice being the soul's greatest good and injustice its greatest evil. He asks Socrates to praise and blame them by what they do to their possessor, stripping away true reputation and adding false, and recalls Socrates' admission that justice is desired for its own sake like sight or knowledge.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Adeimantus (with Glaucon's earlier request quoted)

entries.label: Justice first, then human praise
entries.summary: Socrates says the further question—what poets may say about men—cannot be settled now: their claims that the wicked are often happy, injustice profitable when undetected, and justice a man's own loss are to be forbidden and the opposite sung, but whether such things may be said awaits the discovery of what justice is and how it benefits its possessor, whether he seems just or not.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates, with Adeimantus assenting

entries.label: Justice as one's own work
entries.summary: Hunting justice, Socrates reports it lay under their feet: the founding principle that each man practise the one thing to which his nature is best adapted — doing one's own business and not being a busybody — is justice, or part of it. It is also the residue of the search begun from the assumption that the well-ordered city is wise, valiant, temperate and just, with the fourth virtue the one left after the other three.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IV · dialogue · Socrates, addressed to Glaucon (with Adeimantus earlier agreeing to the one-man-one-work principle)

entries.label: Justice as fourth virtue
entries.summary: Socrates argues that justice is what remains once temperance, courage, and wisdom are identified: it is the cause, condition, and preserver of the other three, and the virtue competing with wisdom, temperance, and courage is justice (a question the interlocutor agrees is not easy to answer).
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IV · dialogue · Socrates (claims); unnamed interlocutor assents

entries.label: Inner harmony is justice
entries.summary: Justice belongs to the inward man: the just person lets no element interfere with another's work but orders his inner life as his own master and law, binding soul, spirit, and appetite into one temperate, harmonious nature -- summarized later as natural order and governance among parts of the soul, with injustice its strife and rebellion (vice being the soul's disease and deformity).
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IV · dialogue · Socrates (account); unnamed interlocutor confirms

entries.label: Ideal as standard
entries.summary: Pressed (by the interlocutor, whom an editorial sidenote calls Glaucon) on whether the proposed state is possible, the speaker replies that the enquiry aimed at an ideal of perfect justice as a standard for judging ourselves, so that an approximate realization satisfies the demand; the interlocutor agrees actuality falls short of the ideal in language.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · Socrates and interlocutor (named Glaucon only in editorial sidenote)

entries.label: Restoring justice's good name
entries.summary: Socrates reports that justice was shown best in itself without its rewards, and now demands that the reputation borrowed away in the argument — that the just man appear unjust — be restored to justice, since she confers reality and not deception.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK X · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Index: justice definitions
entries.summary: Index entry aggregating the Republic's many proposed definitions and characterisations of justice—truth and paying debts, the interest of the stronger, honour among thieves, excellence of the soul, harmony and the union of wisdom, temperance and courage, division of labour, Glaucon's conventionalist account, comparison with health, and its political form in state and individual—ending with absolute justice.
entries.sourceLabel: Index and editorial apparatus · paratext

entries.label: Editorial: justice frames Republic
entries.summary: Editorial note presenting the search for justice as the foundation of the Republic: First Book definitions fail, Glaucon and Adeimantus demand proof justice is a good in itself (I have placed them as speakers of their own reported challenges), and Socrates proposes the state-in-larger-letters so justice appears as the bond of social organization and the principle that each do his own work. The proof runs through the decline from ideal to actual constitutions, culminating in the tyrant's '729 times less pleasure' than the king's, and extends to rewards after death.

entries.summary: Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia
entries.sourceLabel: Summary of source occurrences

entries.label: Republic's scope and method
entries.summary: The commentator calls the Republic Plato's greatest and most wide-ranging work, unique in interweaving life with speculation and politics with philosophy. It is said to contain the germs and first inventions of later logic and psychology (definition, contradiction, essence vs. accidents, division of the soul and of desires) and to insist on the difference between words and things, though Plato himself does not always avoid the confusion, and his logic remains veiled in metaphysics.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · the introduction's commentator

entries.label: Justice and State as one truth
entries.summary: Answering Morgenstern and others on whether defining justice or constructing the State is the work's principal argument, the commentator answers that the two blend in one and are two faces of the same truth: justice is the order of the State, the State the visible embodiment of justice in human society — soul and body of one ideal. Justice then reappears throughout the work as the inner law of the soul and as the principle of rewards and punishments in another life, and rests ultimately on the idea of good.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · the introduction's commentator

entries.label: State-first answer on happiness
entries.summary: Commentary says Socrates' answer is altogether indirect: he dwells on the difficulty of the problem and frames an ideal covering the whole relations of man, reading justice first in the larger letters of society — the State, then the individual. In substance, in the perfect State justice and happiness coincide and happiness may be left to take care of itself once justice is found. The commentary admits some inconsistency with Book X's claim to have got rid of justice's rewards and honours, since those of the perfect State remain, and says the philosopher sheltering behind a wall could hardly be counted happy in this world.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: State precedes the individual
entries.summary: Commentary says Plato preserves the Greek order of beginning with the State and going on to the individual — the reverse of the modern order of ideas — since early individuals knew no good or evil apart from the law of their country or creed of their church. A third remark notes the confusion or identification of individual and State, ethics and politics, pervading early Greek speculation and still dangerous to us: the good man and the good citizen coincide only in the perfect State, which cannot be produced by legislation from without but only, if at all, by education from within.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Luxury, war, and guardians
entries.summary: Analysis traces how a city grown from needs and divided labour becomes, at Glaucon's demand for comforts, a luxurious city whose extra mouths require seizure of neighbours' land and so produce war and a soldier class. Applying the division of labour to war raises the guardian problem: the guardian must combine gentleness toward friends with fierceness toward enemies. The dog, gentle to friends and fierce to strangers because it judges by knowing and not knowing, supplies the image: guardians must be philosophers or lovers of learning, whence the question of their education.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Guardians tested, ranks transferred
entries.summary: Elders who love their subjects and keep their principles under force and pleasure are chosen as guardians, tried like gold refined and honoured as the select class. The accompanying earthborn myth assigns gold, silver and brass-iron natures of rulers, auxiliaries and workers, yet permits a child to rise or fall in rank when its metal differs from its parents', since rule by brass or iron would end the state; an editorial note treats this transposition of ranks as an un-Greek idea clothed in adapted myth.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue

entries.label: Guardians hold no property
entries.summary: The earthborn must live as watchdogs and soldiers rather than shopkeepers, with common meals and pay only covering expenses. They alone may not own houses, land or money, nor handle or drink from gold and silver, which they possess divinely in the soul; acquiring property would turn them into masters and tyrants and bring ruin to themselves and the state.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue

entries.label: Duty before happiness
entries.summary: The analysis reports that the State was founded for its own well-being rather than the citizens' happiness — the citizens are to be guardians, not holiday-makers — and presents this as raising for ancient and modern philosophy the question of duty against happiness and of right against utility.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Utility as second principle
entries.summary: The commentary treats the utilitarian principle as a corrective rather than the historical basis of morality, notes that 'happiness' is ambiguous (pleasure or an ideal life, self or all), and so denies 'the greatest happiness' the rank of foundation of ethics while allowing it as the second principle for actions neither right nor wrong. In politics it calls expediency the law of right limited by the conditions of human society, and reports Plato's order as duty first and happiness later, without excluding utility (the most beneficial also called most honourable and most sacred, v. 457 B, 458 E).
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Tripartite soul, one justice
entries.summary: Using the shorter way in place of the 'truer and longer' one, the report argues from the principle that the same thing cannot be affected oppositely in the same relation: the thirsty soul's simultaneous impulse to drink and forbiddance shows distinct principles (desire and reason), while the story of Leontius at the corpses and the indignation of a generous man suffering unjustly show a third, spirited element that allies with reason yet, existing in children and brutes, is not reason. From this the analysis infers that the virtues of State and individual are the same, justice being each part doing its own work and injustice the insubordination of the inferior parts — a disease of the soul as of the body.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates (reported in the analysis)

entries.label: State/individual fallacy and gain
entries.summary: Editorial critique balanced by concession: Plato's assimilation of state to individual and confusion of ethics with politics rest on a 'partly fallacious' analogy, since a nation's will is a balance or surplus of interacting individual wills and collective action lacks a single man's pliancy; he also misuses verbal analogies (harmony of sounds to harmony of life), though 'through this fallacious medium, a real enlargement of ideas is attained'. Identifying ethics with politics gave both definiteness and moral elevation, its modern separation has its own losses, and 'when the errors against which they were directed have passed away, they in turn become errors'.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentary voice (first person)

entries.label: Search justice in the city first
entries.summary: Socrates proposes the 'large letters' workaround for unaided eyesight: since justice appears both as an individual and a State virtue, and the State is larger, they should seek justice and injustice first in the State and then in the individual, comparing greater with lesser, watching them arise in a constructed State.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Socrates, agreed to by Adeimantus and others

entries.label: Trade, market, hired labour
entries.summary: Socrates (with Adeimantus answering) argues that home production must exceed producers' own needs in quantity and quality so that suppliers can be accommodated; this entails more husbandmen, artisans, merchants and seafarers, and, for exchanging products within the city (a principal object of forming the state), a market-place and money-token; the need for sales when no trading partner is present creates retail-traders and hirelings.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Socrates and Adeimantus

entries.label: Where does justice arise?
entries.summary: Once the state is 'matured and perfected', Socrates asks where justice and injustice arise and in what part of the State they sprang up; Adeimantus suggests probably in the dealings of the citizens with one another, and Socrates agrees to think the enquiry out rather than shrink from it.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Socrates and Adeimantus

entries.label: Healthy versus luxurious city
entries.summary: Socrates sketches the citizens' simple way of life (corn, wine, homespun clothes, barley cakes on leaves, moderation in procreation); when Glaucon objects that even a city of pigs would be fed so and demands sofas, tables and sweets, Socrates says he has described the true and healthy State but will add a 'luxurious State' at fever-heat, since justice and injustice may be more visible there and many will want luxuries beyond necessities, requiring painter and embroiderer, gold, ivory and more.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Socrates, with Glaucon interjecting

entries.label: Luxury leads to war
entries.summary: Socrates argues that the healthy State must be enlarged with callings answering no natural want (huntings and actors, poets and rhapsodists, cooks, confectioners, etc.) and more physicians; the territory then becomes insufficient, so each city will want a slice of its neighbour's land if it pursues unlimited accumulation of wealth, and war follows — war being derived here from causes said to be behind almost all evils in cities, public and private (Socrates withholds any judgment whether war does good or harm).
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Socrates with Adeimantus (and editorial sidenotes summarizing the argument)

entries.label: One art per man: war
entries.summary: Applying the earlier principle that one man cannot practise many arts with success, Socrates argues that war is an art demanding as much attention as shoemaking and cannot be left to a farmer or artisan; since nobody becomes a competent player or craftsman at odd moments, and no tool makes an untrained man skilful, the fighting must be done by specialists with natural aptitude, from whom the city's guardians must be selected.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Socrates with an interlocutor

entries.label: Gentle yet spirited guardians
entries.summary: Guardians need bodily speed and strength and a soul full of spirit (as in dogs), yet spirited natures tend to be savage; they must be dangerous to enemies and gentle to friends, which seems a contradiction. Socrates points to well-bred dogs, gentle to familiars and hostile to strangers, as proof such natures exist; he further credits the dog with philosophy because it likes and dislikes by knowledge and ignorance, so the good guardian must unite philosophy, spirit, swiftness and strength.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Socrates with Glaucon/Adeimantus; sidenote editorial summaries alongside

entries.label: Question: who shall rule?
entries.summary: Socrates closes the account of nurture and education, saying the general principle already found settles details like dances and contests, and then asks the next question: who must be rulers and who subjects.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates (dialogue figure, not authorial endorsement)

entries.label: Elders and the loyal must rule
entries.summary: The elder is to rule the younger and the best guardians the rest; candidates are noted who through their whole lives are most eager to benefit the country and averse to harming it, on the stated premise that people care for what they believe shares their interests and affects their own fortune.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates (dialogue figure, not authorial endorsement)

entries.label: Trials and tests for guardians
entries.summary: Candidates are watched from youth and set actions, toils, pains and conflicts in which they are most likely to forget or be deceived, and finally passed through terrors and pleasures to be proved like gold in a furnace; whoever holds the conviction of the State's interest at every age is appointed ruler and honoured in life and death, and failures are rejected.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates (dialogue figure, not authorial endorsement)

entries.label: Royal lie: earth-born metals
entries.summary: Socrates proposes a needful falsehood, a single royal lie told first to the rulers, then the soldiers, then the people: their upbringing was a dream and they were formed in and born from the earth as brethren, and of gold, silver, or brass and iron, with mixed-nature children transposed up or down in rank and an oracle warning of ruin if a base metal rules the State.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates (dialogue figure, not authorial endorsement)

entries.label: Fiction credible to descendants?
entries.summary: Glaucon answers that the tale cannot be believed by the present generation but perhaps by their sons and later posterity; Socrates grants the difficulty yet claims that such a belief would make citizens care more for the city and for one another before turning to other matters.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Glaucon and Socrates (dialogue figures, not authorial endorsement)

entries.label: Auxiliaries may turn to tyrants
entries.summary: Auxiliaries, being stronger than the citizens, might cease to be friends and allies and become savage tyrants — like watch-dogs that turn and worry the sheep — so great care is required, and Socrates (correcting Glaucon's confidence) holds that true education, whatever it be, best civilizes and humanizes them.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates (dialogue figure, not authorial endorsement)

entries.label: Happiness of the whole city
entries.summary: Socrates answers that the guardians may in fact be the happiest of men, but the state is founded for the happiness of the whole, not of one class; like a statue, each feature must keep its proportion rather than be beautified out of its function. If guardians chase private luxury they cease to be guardians and turn the state upside down, so each class must do its own work and receive the share happiness nature assigns.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IV · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Wealth and poverty spoil crafts
entries.summary: Socrates claims two causes degrade the arts: wealth makes the potter indolent and careless; poverty leaves him without tools and unable to work or teach his sons and apprentices. So workers and their work degenerate under either condition. Wealth and poverty are therefore evils for the guardians to prevent — luxury and indolence on one side, meanness and viciousness on the other, both productive of discontent.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IV · dialogue · Socrates, with Adeimantus assenting

entries.label: State–individual parallel
entries.summary: Socrates claims the constitutions of states vary as the dispositions of men vary, since states are made not of 'oak and rock' but of the human natures in them; Glaucon agrees that states grow out of human characters. They therefore keep the old method of taking the State first and then its corresponding individual for each form.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VIII · dialogue · Socrates and Glaucon

entries.label: Whole's happiness secures the parts
entries.summary: The editor reports that when Adeimantus objects to the citizens' harsh garrison-like life (Republic 4. 419), Socrates answers that if the happiness of the whole is secured the happiness of the parts follows; this is cited as one mark of the older Hellenic element, with the individual subordinated to the state.

entries.summary: The city-first method and the State–soul analogy: an indirect answer and a method that is contested even by its own editor
entries.sourceLabel: Summary of source occurrences

entries.label: God is good: censoring the tales
entries.summary: In the guardians' education through music and literature, the reports say nursery tales must be censored because children must not learn what they will later unlearn, and Homer and Hesiod tell immoral falsehoods. Two principles govern: God must be represented as the author of good only, not of evil; and with God is no change of form or variableness — God is true, never deceiving by word or sign, so the poets' shape-shifting and lying divine dreams must be suppressed.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Narrative kinds and imitation
entries.summary: Analysis reports that narrative is of three kinds — simple, imitative, or mixed (the opening of Homer illustrating the mixed kind) — and that guardians should not be imitators at all, since one man cannot play many parts; if they imitate anything it must be the good, for the actor's mask tends to become his face. The descriptive style with little imitation suits a self-respecting man, while the man without self-respect imitates anybody and anything; the complex polyphonic performer is received with respect but told there is no room for his kind in this State.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Music trains taste before reason
entries.summary: The analysis holds that music enters the deepest part of the soul and instils a sense of beauty and deformity before reason appears; the person so trained then welcomes reason as a friend already known. It compares this to learning letters before combinations and speaks of a music of the soul answering the harmony of the world, ending that true love is born of temperance.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue

entries.label: Plain diet and simple cures
entries.summary: Treating soul as cause and body as effect, the passage leaves bodily training in the educated mind's charge and prescribes abstention from wine, plain gymnastics and plain food modelled on Homer's heroes; luxury breeds doctors and litigation-lovers. Asclepius' quick cure-or-kill method suits workers who cannot afford illness, rejecting the nursing of chronic self-indulgent disease associated with Herodicus.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue

entries.label: Judge must know vice from outside
entries.summary: With Glaucon raising the question of experience, Socrates distinguishes the physician, who may know disease in his own body because he heals with mind, from the judge, whose mind must not be corrupted by crime since mind rules mind. The judge should reach middle age innocent and learn evil only by observing others, and such medicine and law would treat only better natures while music and gymnastics reduce the need for both.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · Socrates (as summarized)

entries.label: Arts map to reason and passion
entries.summary: Both works concern the soul (one taming, one arousing and sustaining it), not soul and body as the earlier level implies. Excess gymnastics hardens the spirited nature into beast-like stupidity, excess music melts away spiritedness; the two arts correspond rather to reason and passion in man, and he who mingling them in concord is the true musician presiding over the state.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue

entries.label: Editor doubts innocence claim
entries.summary: The editorial note questions whether this reasoning holds: it cites Laws xii. 950 B as admitting that the evil can estimate the good correctly, suggests insight into vice may coexist with abhorrence of it, and holds that knowledge of character is partly a natural capacity independent of special experience of good or evil.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Religion left to Apollo
entries.summary: A quoted claim says that after legislation only the ordering of religion remains and is left to Apollo at Delphi, the ancestral deity, with no foreign god supreme. The surrounding commentary itself says religion is passed over lightly once two principles are secured: the highest conception of the gods and maintenance of the Hellenic national type.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Simplicity in medicine and law
entries.summary: The commentator reads Plato as urging simplicity in medicine and law alike: modern physicians, gaining in analysis of parts, lose their grasp of the frame as a whole and overcomplicate disease, while in law the greater matters go to the legislator or the oracle of Delphi and the lesser to the citizens themselves. State ills, like hydra heads, are best prevented by care of education rather than extirpated. The commentator also faults Plato's depreciation of diet and his willingness to let invalids die.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentator (introduction/analysis)

entries.label: Music first; tales censored
entries.summary: Guardians' education follows the traditional two divisions, gymnastic for the body and music for the soul, music (including literature, true and false) coming first because fictitious stories are told to children before gymnastics; since the beginning forms character most readily, children must not hear casual tales, and a censorship of writers of fiction must accept good tales and reject bad ones for mothers and nurses to use, discarding most tales now in circulation.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Socrates with Adeimantus; embedded sidenotes give editorial headings

entries.label: God is good, changeless, true
entries.summary: Modelled on the truths of the framed laws, poets must represent God as truly is: since God is good and the good does no evil and is the cause of well-being, God is the author only of good, so the causes of human evils must be sought elsewhere (though just punishment may be attributed to God). Further, things at their best are least altered, so God neither takes many shapes nor changes himself, and — the true lie being ignorance of highest matters in the soul, its verbal form only an imitation — no motive or need for deception could apply to God, who is simple and true in word and deed; poets' tales asserting the contrary are to be barred from the State and from teaching.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK II · dialogue · Socrates with Adeimantus; embedded sidenotes and footnotes give editorial commentary

entries.label: Some tales told, others withheld
entries.summary: Socrates states the rule carried over from Book II: from their youth, disciples must hear some tales and not others, if they are to honour gods and parents and value friendship; Adeimantus agrees the principles are right.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates, with Adeimantus assenting

entries.label: Underworld tales banished
entries.summary: Since belief in a real and terrible world below destroys courage, narrators must commend rather than revile it; Homer's verses on gloomy Hades, mindless shades and shrieking souls are to be struck out—its poetical charm makes them more unfit for free men, who should fear slavery more than death—and terrifying names such as Cocytus and Styx are likewise dropped in favour of a nobler strain.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates, with Adeimantus assenting

entries.label: Lament for the dead banished
entries.summary: From the principle that the good man does not fear death for a good comrade, is sufficient for himself, and so feels loss least, weepings of famous men are to be assigned to women or baser men; Homer must not show Achilles or Priam rolling in the dirt and wailing, still less the gods lamenting, since youths who take such scenes seriously, instead of laughing at them, lose shame and self-control and whine on slight occasions.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates, with Adeimantus assenting

entries.label: Lying as rulers' medicine
entries.summary: Truth is highly valued: a lie is useless to the gods and, like medicine, belongs to the physician—here the rulers, who alone may lie for the public good against enemies or citizens; any other liar in the state, whether priest, physician or carpenter, is a fault worse than a patient hiding his illness from his doctor, and is to be punished as one who subverts ship or state.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates, with Adeimantus assenting

entries.label: Crimes of heroes rejected
entries.summary: Socrates declines to believe Achilles took gifts, ransomed Hector's body for pay, defied Apollo and the river-god, and slaughtered captives, and refuses the tales of Theseus and Peirithous' violent rape: poets must declare either that these deeds were not done or that their doers were not sons of gods—not both at once—lest hearers excuse their own vices by the example of god-born kin and morals loosen among the young.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates, with Adeimantus assenting

entries.label: Narration, imitation, or mixture
entries.summary: Poetry and myth narrate events, but narration may be simple, imitative, or mixed: the poet imitates when he assimilates himself to another's voice and gesture (as Homer takes Chryses' part after the opening lines of the Iliad) and drops into simple narration when he speaks throughout in his own person; tragedy and comedy are wholly imitative, the dithyramb purely narrative, epic and some other kinds a combination.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates, with Adeimantus answering

entries.label: Guardians' imitation confined
entries.summary: Since one man can do only one thing well, guardians may not imitate many parts: imitation continued from youth becomes a second nature in body, voice and mind, so they may imitate only suitable characters—the courageous, temperate, holy, free and the like—and not women in distress, slaves, cowards, madmen or craftsmen; the good man's style mixes much narration with little imitation, and the versatile pantomimic poet is honoured and garlanded but sent to another city.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates, with Adeimantus assenting

entries.label: Two austere harmonies kept
entries.summary: Asked for harmonies fitting a man's bearing in danger and necessity and in persuasion and moderate success, 'I' asks to keep only those two strains; the interlocutor identifies them as the Dorian and Phrygian.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates (asker); interlocutor supplies the names

entries.label: Lyre and harp only
entries.summary: Because the retained harmonies need no panharmonic scale, many-stringed makers are dropped and the flute is refused outright; only lyre and harp remain in the city, with a pipe allowed to country shepherds.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates with agreeing interlocutor

entries.label: Words govern style and rhythm
entries.summary: Rhythms should express a courageous and orderly life, with foot and melody adapted to words rather than words to them; good and bad rhythm and harmony follow style, and style depends on the temper of the soul.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Simplicity as style's root
entries.summary: Beauty of style, harmony, grace, and good rhythm rest on the true simplicity of a rightly and nobly ordered mind, expressly distinguished from the simplicity that is a euphemism for folly; a later exchange calls simplicity in music the parent of temperance and simplicity in gymnastic the parent of health.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Beauty shapes guardians early
entries.summary: All creative arts must depict only the good and graceful or be barred, so that guardians do not graze on images of deformity; rhythm and harmony reach the soul's inward places, forming taste to love the good before reason arrives and then to recognise it as an old friend.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates, addressing Glaucon

entries.label: Judge learns evil secondhand
entries.summary: Physicians may know disease from their own bodies, since they cure body by mind; judges govern mind by mind and so must be old, uncorrupted in youth, and taught of vice only by long observation of others, for vice cannot know virtue while a virtuous nature knows both.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Education as the one care
entries.summary: Socrates says the earlier regulations are trifles as long as the one thing is cared for: education and nurture. Well-educated citizens will settle omitted matters (marriage, holding women and children in common) for themselves, and a well-started state runs on like a wheel — good nurture implanting good constitutions, which in a good education improve further and even improve the breed.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IV · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Musical change, legal change
entries.summary: Socrates (citing Damon, with Adeimantus's agreement) says music and gymnastic must be kept in their original form, because any musical innovation is dangerous to the whole state — when modes change, the fundamental laws change with them. Adeimantus describes licence entering as harmless amusement and spreading through manners into contracts, laws and constitutions at last overthrowing all rights; the habit of order gained in music and play is set against this drift.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IV · dialogue · Socrates and Adeimantus; Damon reported by Socrates

entries.label: Editor's conception of art
entries.summary: A bracketed editor's note asserts that for Plato art is not canons of criticism but an all-pervading influence, judged solely by simplicity as moderation, purity and proportion, with censorship extended from poetry and music to sculpture and architecture; the note contrasts the Republic's austere ideal with Protag. 311 C and Meno 91 D on Pheidias.
entries.sourceLabel: Index and editorial apparatus · paratext · editorial commentator

entries.label: Editorial: God across Republic/Laws
entries.summary: Editorial note summing up the Republic's theology under two heads—God is perfect and unchangeable, and God is true and the author of truth—and presenting these as the canons by which poetry is judged. The editor adds that Plato later hardens (Laws) but repeats many Republic theses (God is not the author of evil, will not favor the unjust), and that the Demiurge of Timaeus, Sophist and Statesman hardly appears in Republic or Laws.
entries.sourceLabel: Index and editorial apparatus · paratext

entries.label: Music in the wide sense
entries.summary: Editorial commentary states that Greek 'music' meant mental training opposed to gymnastic, spanning reading and writing, mathematics, harmony and poetry (drawing being sometimes a separate division, per Aristotle). It says Plato places music before gymnastic and treats strictly musical education as shaping harmonious character and true conceptions of good and evil rather than idle pleasure or virtuoso performance.
entries.sourceLabel: Index and editorial apparatus · paratext · editor (bracketed index commentary)

entries.label: Against novelty in music
entries.summary: The editor states that Plato's simplicity and fixity in music (restricted instruments and modes, no change in musical fashion) probably opposed the ornate tendencies of his own age, and that Plato treated that change as a cause rather than a sign of Hellas' decline. The editor dissents from Plato's view, judging the change 'inevitable, and not perhaps wholly to be regretted' — an explicit editorial difference from the author it describes.

entries.label: Education
entries.summary: Forming character by nurture: music, gymnastics, restricted stories, and the limits of law
entries.sourceLabel: Summary of source occurrences

entries.label: Women share guardian training
entries.summary: The report has Socrates give women guardians the same employments as men and therefore the same music, gymnastic and military training, discounting ridicule of their exercises as mere habit. Against the charge of contradicting the division of labour (differences of nature warranting different uses), he argues that the male/female difference is partial, like bald versus hairy or male versus female physician, unlike the whole-nature difference of physician and carpenter: begetting and bearing children do not entail different education, aptitudes are scattered among both sexes, and the apt women should be chosen as guardians.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates (reported in the analysis)

entries.label: Community of wives and children
entries.summary: Book V's second and larger wave: the commentary frames a demand, voiced by Polemarchus and Adeimantus, for an explanation of the communal arrangement of women and children, and reports Socrates separating what is possible from what is desirable. After the first wave yields the admission that men and women have common duties, the second wave asks whether community of wives and children is expedient or possible, and is to be sketched first as 'a dream of what might be' before returning to what can be.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates (reported in the analysis)

entries.label: Regulated pairing, hidden parents
entries.summary: The analyst reports Socrates' scheme: the rulers pair good with good and bad with bad through fixed marriage festivals and rigged lots, rear one offspring and destroy the other, conceal parentage so no mother recognises her child; ages are fixed (men 25-55, women 20-40) and kinship—parents, brothers, sisters—is reckoned from espousals and births dated to the festivals.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · paratext · Socrates (as paraphrased by the analyst, with quoted exchanges of Glaucon)

entries.label: Unity as the state's greatest good
entries.summary: Offered as proof that the scheme is advantageous: the greatest good of a state is unity and its evil discord, achieved when all share pleasures, pains and interests; shared property, common family names meant 'not mere words' and even the permission to strike remove property suits and flattery without sacrificing individual happiness; carried further, Hellenes count as one family, so war between them is civil quarrel to be waged only against the guilty few and with a view to reconciliation.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · paratext · Socrates (as paraphrased by the analyst)

entries.label: Editor's defects of Book V
entries.summary: In the editor's own remarks: the communal plan leaves its application to the lower classes unstated and its kinship prohibitions fail (siblings defined by seven- or nine-month birth cohorts cannot be reliably identified; the manipulation of the lots is unexplained); separately, the new doctrine of 'contingent matter' is criticised as confusing the contingent with the relative and degrees of knowledge with degrees of being, a confusion he says begins to clear in the Theaetetus and the Sophist.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · paratext

entries.label: Paradoxes of the perfect State
entries.summary: Opening the survey, the commentator says Plato's perfect State is full of paradox by ordinary standards: moderns have sneered at its proposals as absurd or immoral or taken comfort in Aristotle's criticisms. But errors with a side of truth, and truths mixed with error (where 'the half is better than the whole'), may still be a contribution to the study of human nature and deserve careful treatment rather than alarm about existing institutions.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · editorial commentator (Introduction)

entries.label: Community of goods and critics
entries.summary: The first paradox is community of goods, mentioned briefly at the end of Book III and, as Aristotle observes, seemingly confined to the guardians — an omission the commentator attributes to the plan of the work rather than to significance. Aristotle censures common property as repressing industry and benevolence, and modern writers treat the question as already settled by mankind's common opinion. Against this the commentator urges that the sacredness of property is far more fixed in modern than in ancient times, when debt, war, revolution and legislation made holdings insecure, and that even early Christians held goods in common.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · editorial commentator (Introduction)

entries.label: Equal work and training for women
entries.summary: Plato prefaces community of wives with a proposal that men and women take the same occupations and training. The apparent clash with the rule that different natures choose different pursuits (and with the division of labour) is answered within his scheme: the only organic difference is that men beget and women bear children, natural gifts being scattered indifferently between the sexes (with at most a difference of degree), and the indecency objection is answered as mere habit. The commentator concedes the modern counter that the differences of sensibility and energy 'affect the whole nature', but holds it unclear how far these are produced by education, inherited custom and mode of life, so that Plato 'may have been right' to admit no ultimate difference beyond that which exists in animals.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · editorial commentator (Introduction), reporting and contending with Plato

entries.label: Marriage as race-breeding
entries.summary: The second paradox, community of wives and children, is put as 'Is it possible? Is it desirable?' with Glaucon's doubts and stronger doubts of the commentator's. The commentator first reconstructs Plato's motives: the relations intended are an impossible strictness rather than licence, the family is treated as the natural enemy of the state in hope of an universal brotherhood, and pairing is directed solely to improvement of the race, with only the fitter lives preserved. The same passage then refuses the ideal in the name of Christian care for the weakest — infant, criminal, insane — and the endless value of the individual, so that to a modern and Christian view Plato is 'sanctioning murder and destroying the first principles of morality'.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · editorial commentator (Introduction), reporting Plato and Glaucon

entries.label: Man exceeds the animal analogy
entries.summary: The commentator argues that the great error of these speculations is forgetting the difference between man and the animals: humans are viewed as by a dog- or bird-fancier, and improvement is taken to be size, flesh and strength, whereas human improvement is the growth of mind — so there must be 'a marriage of true minds', which the scheme destroys along with all parental and conjugal affection, though even the nobler animals (Plato's own illustration) remain faithful and nurse their young. Parallel claim: life should rest on a moral rather than a physical basis, mind caring for both body and mind, with the moral as the expansion of the physical and no health of mind without duty and love of truth.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · editorial commentator (Introduction)

entries.label: Monogamy and the family defended
entries.summary: The commentator appeals to history against the Platonic marriage: wherever polygamy prevailed the race deteriorated, 'one man to one woman' has once taken by civilized peoples never been retraced, and close intermarriage tends to weakness in children — evidence that morality asserts its authority in the relations of the sexes. Against recent anthropological inference from primitive tribes he protests that the social record is fragmentary and that monogamous care of young in animals cuts the other way. Yet if marriage grew historically out of barbarian selfishness, its idea has been progressively defined and consecrated (East, Greeks and Romans, Christian nations); that view supplies a firmer reason to hold it sacred, with a warning not to abandon moral principle in the uncertainty of transitional knowledge.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · editorial commentator (Introduction)

entries.label: Heredity cannot breed genius
entries.summary: The closing argument denies that artificial breeding can improve mankind: strength and health are not the only goods, mind and character matter more, and the problem is complex (four generations back yield some thirty progenitors) while true inheritance of genius cannot be distinguished from imitation and circumstance. Great men and women have rarely had great parents, and the descendants of the English poets are undistinguished, so the fancy that matched pairings could produce a Shakespeare or Milton is ridiculed. Many of the noblest were physically weak (Tyrtaeus, Aesop, Newton), and mankind passed from brutal to civilized marriage not by pairing strong with strong or dissimilar natures, but by other means.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · editorial commentator (Introduction)

entries.label: Heredity limited by the will
entries.summary: Editorial argument: inherited mental and physical qualities, popularly noticed in families, can be neither measured nor make up much of a person. Foreknowledge of family disease can guide prevention, so heredity, 'from being a curse, may become a blessing', and within the wall of necessity the will can still 'creat[e] a life for ourselves'.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentary voice (first person)

entries.label: Family: nurture and cost
entries.summary: Opposed editorial claims held together: children cannot be reared outside families ('a subtle sympathy between the mother and the child'), so Plato's all-foundling state would mostly perish, 'so emphatically does nature protest against the destruction of the family'; yet family attachments do 'interfere with higher aims', diverting people from country or the ideal, so Plato is credited (though not morally defended) with showing the reverse side of the picture.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentary voice (first person)

entries.label: Genius smothered by uniformity
entries.summary: Editorial claim: Plato misapplied Sparta—Spartan physique owed chiefly to temperance and training, not marriage law; Sparta's fixed laws allowed no individual to rise above the state, and it lacked Athens' greatness (its 'genius... the love of liberty'). Progress in cities and nations comes from remarkable individuals whose origins we cannot control, and systems that extinguish such 'sparks of genius and character' deserve strong condemnation.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentary voice (first person)

entries.label: Population and marital prudence
entries.summary: Editorial argument: 'Population is the most untameable force in the political and social world'; improvident marriage worsens poverty (large cities, India, Ireland) and generates sickly descendants, yet the passions outrun prudence and wisdom is lost 'just in that action of our lives in which we have the most need of it', so remedies are mainly indirect. Rare individuals (Dr. Combe; a friend wearing a black ribbon as a warning against marriage owing to inherited insanity) did from duty what others should; such marriages ought if possible to be prevented and might come to carry a 'horror naturalis', but law is unenforceable and, the commentary concedes, reason seldom overcomes 'the irresistible impulse of individual attachment'.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentary voice (first person), with quoted dramatic line

entries.label: Plato's all-sufficing State
entries.summary: Editorial analysis of Plato's political idea: where we see the State as built up from or enclosing family life, Plato treats the family as 'a disturbing influence' against the State's higher unity; no organization but a political (and military) one is needed, and the citizen's whole life is war, preparation for war, and, in old age, philosophy. The commentator finds 'an element of monasticism even in Plato's communism' and notes that the Laws (v. 739 B) does not retract the error, permitting marriage only through 'the infirmity of mankind'.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentary voice (first person), analyzing Plato's position

entries.label: Guardian regimen: no gold, no land
entries.summary: Guardians are to live like soldiers in a camp: no private property, houses or stores, only fixed yearly provisions from the citizens for trained, temperate warriors, and gold and silver forbidden to them; failure of these rules, the passage argues, turns guardians into husbandmen, tyrants and enemies who fear their fellow citizens more than foreign foes and bring ruin to the State.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK III · dialogue · Socrates (dialogue figure, not authorial endorsement)

entries.label: Guardians poor and unpaid
entries.summary: Adeimantus voices a critic: though the city is theirs, its guardians are kept poor, like mercenaries who only mount guard. Socrates extends the charge — they are fed but not paid, so they cannot travel for pleasure or spend on a mistress or other luxuries counted as happiness. A footnote gives an alternative sense of the charge (that they are made miserable 'for their own good').
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IV · dialogue · Adeimantus voicing an unnamed critic; Socrates replies

entries.label: Objection: each does own work
entries.summary: Voiced in opponents' mouths, the objection holds that the state's foundation assigned everyone the one work suited to their nature, and since the natures of men and women differ greatly, giving them the same actions is a serious inconsistency — against which Socrates asks Glaucon for a defence.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · Socrates voicing unnamed opponents, answered by Glaucon

entries.label: Community of wives and children
entries.summary: The second and greater wave: the law is that guardians' wives and children are to be common, no parent knowing their own child nor child its parent. Glaucon disputes both utility and possibility; Socrates, asking only to day-dream, argues usefulness first and defers the question of possibility.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · Socrates, answered by Glaucon

entries.label: Kinship redefined by cohort
entries.summary: Since no one can know actual parentage, kinship is redefined by co-timing: after a given hymeneal, children born in the seventh and tenth month are called that bridegroom's sons and daughters, and a whole wedded cohort's children are called brothers and sisters and barred from intermarriage, along with lines of descent each way; an exception is allowed where the lot favours and the Pythian oracle consents.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · Socrates, answered by Glaucon

entries.label: Disputes over 'mine'
entries.summary: The speaker claims that social differences commonly begin in disagreement over the application of 'mine', 'not mine', 'his', 'not his', and proposes as the best-ordered state the one where the greatest number apply these terms alike to the same thing.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · Socrates and unnamed interlocutor

entries.label: City as one body
entries.summary: The best state is compared to a single organism whose whole frame feels a hurt finger's pain: when one citizen fares well or ill, the whole state takes the case as its own. The interlocutor ('he') agrees this common feeling is the greatest good.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · Socrates and unnamed interlocutor

entries.label: Guardians as one family
entries.summary: Guardians are to meet one another only as brother, sister, father, mother, or their issue, and the question is raised whether these family names must be backed by the corresponding care, reverence, and duty, so that the names are honoured in deed as well as lip.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · Socrates and unnamed interlocutor

entries.label: Community of wives, children
entries.summary: The speaker claims the guardians' community of women and children is the chief reason for their shared pleasures and pains and is therefore 'clearly the source of the greatest good to the State'.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · Socrates and unnamed interlocutor

entries.label: No private property
entries.summary: Recalling the rule that guardians hold no houses, lands, or property but live on public maintenance, the speaker argues that community of property and of families prevents the city being torn over 'mine' and 'not mine' and removes the occasions for lawsuits and quarrels.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · Socrates and unnamed interlocutor

entries.label: Editor on Platonic community
entries.summary: A bracketed editor's note argues that the Republic's communism expresses a desire for state unity (5.462 foll.), notes that Plato evades its practicability by the philosopher-ruler remedy, and traces its trajectory through Critias (common property but no community of women) and Laws 5.739 (a second-best state conceding property), quoting Aristotle Pol. ii. 6 on Plato's partial reversion to the ideal polity.
entries.sourceLabel: Index and editorial apparatus · paratext · editorial commentator

entries.label: Republic's state: two mixed elements
entries.summary: Editor's index commentary argues that the polity Plato sketches in the Republic combines two elements — an older Hellenic, partly Spartan-type state (small citizen body, subordination of individual to state, war as normal condition) and an ideal city of common possessions ruled by philosopher-rulers chosen by merit — and that, as Aristotle complained, the two are not perfectly combined and much is left ill-defined.
entries.sourceLabel: Index and editorial apparatus · paratext · index editor (editorial commentary)

entries.label: Three peculiar institutions
entries.summary: The editor singles out three features as most peculiar to Plato's state: community of property (paralleled at most by Sparta, Crete, or the Pythagorean brotherhood), the position of women, and government by philosophers.
entries.sourceLabel: Index and editorial apparatus · paratext · index editor (editorial commentary)

entries.label: Women's place vs Hellenic custom
entries.summary: The editor judges that nothing in the Republic would have struck contemporaries more than Plato's assignment to women of common marriage, equal education, war service, and administration — worse to Athenian eyes than the reputed licence of Spartan women, whose public influence was indirect and who held no office or arms, while upper-class Athenian women lived in seclusion. The index entry 'Women' gathers the corresponding loci (training like men, gymnasium, war, guardianship, common wives and children) and points back to this State article.
entries.sourceLabel: Index and editorial apparatus · paratext · index editor (editorial commentary)
