entries.label: Guardian institutions
entries.summary: The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods
entries.sourceLabel: Summary of source occurrences

entries.label: Kings must be philosophers
entries.summary: Pressed by Glaucon to say whether the ideal state is possible, the analyst's Socrates concedes that nature never fully realizes the ideal, but reduces the required change to one—'Until, then, kings are philosophers, or philosophers are kings, cities will never cease from ill'—and begins to say who these philosophers and rulers are.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · paratext · Glaucon and Socrates (as reported in dialogue form by the analyst)

entries.label: Knowledge of forms vs opinion
entries.summary: To separate true philosophers from lovers of sights, the analyst's Socrates posits unchanging abstract ideas (justice, beauty, good) as objects of unerring knowledge, while opinion has a third, intermediate object that both is and is not—the ambiguous sensibles whose relativities shift into one another; those grovelling in sense are lovers of opinion only.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · paratext · Socrates (as paraphrased by the analyst, addressing an unnamed challenger)

entries.label: Philosophers turn rogues in fact
entries.summary: Adeimantus objects that, argument apart, the men who make philosophy their life generally turn out rogues if bad and fools if good; the analyst's Socrates agrees he is right, and the objection is pressed as a difficulty for the doctrine that philosophers should be kings.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · paratext · Adeimantus and Socrates (as reported by the analyst)

entries.label: Ship parable; public opinion corrupts
entries.summary: Socrates' reply attributes philosophy's uselessness to states: in the parable, mutineers who drug and bind the near-blind captain call the true navigator fool and star-gazer when he claims rule; further, rare philosophical natures are destroyed because good qualities become evils in bad conditions, public opinion is 'the real Sophist' whose praise and hisses drown education (with exile or death for resisters), and flattered talents or diverted gifts leave philosophy to pretenders—so a world that believes only in plurality cannot but persecute philosophers.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · paratext · Socrates (as paraphrased by the analyst)

entries.label: Guardians must know the good
entries.summary: The analysis turns to the guardians' education: they must be philosophers and take the long road beyond the four virtues to the idea of good, without which worldly gain and seeming virtue profit nothing; the good is rejected as wisdom (a circle) and as pleasure (there are bad pleasures), and Socrates, unable to state it, offers its 'child'—the sun as cause of light and truth in the visible world—and the divided line of the visible and intelligible spheres as the scheme of its grades.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · paratext · Socrates and Glaucon (as reported in dialogue form by the analyst)

entries.label: Idea of good as sun
entries.summary: Socrates, in the paraphrased dialogue, refuses to define the good directly and offers a likening: as the sun gives light and sustains visible things, so the idea of good is the cause of knowledge and truth and of being, itself 'above knowledge and above truth.'
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates (within paraphrased dialogue)

entries.label: Divided line and faculties
entries.summary: Socrates' image divides visible and intelligible worlds into four graded segments — shadows, natural artefacts, hypothetical mathematics, and dialectic ascending to the idea of good — with four corresponding faculties (perception of shadows, faith, active intelligence, pure intelligence).
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates (within paraphrased dialogue)

entries.label: Best natures most corruptible
entries.summary: Replying to Adeimantus' charge that philosophers are useless or rogues, Socrates admits the fact and argues that the best nature is most liable to corruption by alien conditions; the commentator illustrates with temperaments such as poets and men of genius, who may do great evil or great good, and with institutions that sweep fine natures into self-serving loyalty.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates (within paraphrased dialogue); introduction's author elaborating

entries.label: Corruption thesis qualified
entries.summary: The commentator denies the maxim 'corruptio optimi pessima' any general force: conditions that spoil one nature may cultivate another, adverse settings may spur reformers as well as destroy fine natures, and outcomes range 'into great good... into great evil... into both.'
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · introduction's author

entries.label: Higher method left unrealized
entries.summary: The commentator reports Plato's envisaged higher method — ideas as self-supporting steps forming a whole, with consistency as the test of truth — while judging it never practised or explained by Plato, who 'hastens on to the end of the intellectual world' without a science to climb through.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · introduction's author

entries.label: Cave: conversion and return
entries.summary: In the reported parable, chained cave-dwellers know only shadows until an ascent grounds them by stages in the sun, identified with the idea of good; teaching is not giving sight but turning the soul toward the light (conversion), and once enlightened the reluctant philosopher must be compelled to return and rule, since rulers must not desire rule (with the commentator's gloss mapping the cave onto fire as sun and the ascent as the way to knowledge).
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates (within paraphrased dialogue)

entries.label: Number conducts the soul to being
entries.summary: Socrates answers how rulers are made: philosophy converts the soul from night to day, and number or calculation, though it has practical and military uses, is chiefly a conductor to thought and being, teaching by pure abstraction rather than material units.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · Socrates (with Glaucon assenting)

entries.label: Contradiction in sense awakens thought
entries.summary: Three equally seen fingers cannot be distinguished without number; great and small appear confused, and it is the mind that supplies the contrast, so perceived contradiction (the one also opposite of one) is what sets reflection in motion and leads from the visible to the intelligible.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Geometry must look upward to being
entries.summary: Socrates claims geometry's chief use is helping toward contemplation of the idea of good and true being; current practice is derided for aiming downwards at action and the arts rather than at eternal existence, despite its lesser military uses admitted by Glaucon.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · Socrates (Glaucon replying)

entries.label: Astronomy and harmonics by problems
entries.summary: Star-gazing and audible tuning are rejected as knowledge: astronomy must be pursued by problems rather than the heavens, and Pythagorean harmonists fall short by studying only heard consonances, not the unseen numerical harmony found in problems — all with a view to the good.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · Socrates (Glaucon replying)

entries.label: Dialectic: prelude to the idea of good
entries.summary: The mathematical sciences are only a prelude and a dream or hypothesis of true being; dialectic alone rises above hypotheses, distinguishes each nature's essence and the good, and its ascent is set out as the proportion being:becoming :: intellect:opinion, with reason, understanding, faith and shadow-perception as its four terms.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · Socrates (Glaucon questioning)

entries.label: Age-staged training of rulers
entries.summary: Guardians must be naturally able, balanced in mind and body, and young: at twenty the promising are selected to relate the sciences to true being, at thirty those able to abstract enter dialectic for five or six years, then fifteen years of practical service in the den, and at fifty they turn to the idea of good and take turns governing and training successors.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · Socrates (Glaucon replying)

entries.label: Premature dialectic unmoors the young
entries.summary: Socrates warns that dialectic can do evil when taken up too early: like a supposititious son rejecting reputed parents, a young man whose received principles are questioned abandons them for pleasure and lawlessness, so philosophy should begin in sobriety around thirty. Women are to share the training, and the State becomes real once philosopher-kings arise.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · Socrates (Glaucon replying)

entries.label: Particulars can also be true
entries.summary: The commentator argues that Plato's preference for universals is illusory: an individual man or bed is no more erroneous than its class, universals may be false while particulars are true, and Greek ambiguity about opinion and sensation bred Plato's denial of truth to sense-particulars.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Education for the whole of life
entries.summary: Editorial account of Plato's education as partly Greek and partly ideal: he is the first to say education 'is to comprehend the whole of life, and to be a preparation for another in which education begins again (vi. 498 D)'—'the continuous thread' of the Republic and most applicable to modern life. Views have shifted from the Protagoras (virtue teachable; one virtue thesis modified) while Socratic residues remain: education 'implant[s] a principle of intelligence... better than ten thousand eyes', is 'not... the filling of a vessel, but... the turning the eye of the soul towards the light', and 'centre[s] all goodness in the contemplation of the idea of good'. On gymnastic, both music and gymnastic aim at the mind and the lower serves the higher, though strict separation of body and mind training is judged mistaken.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentary voice (first person)

entries.label: Mathematics trains abstraction
entries.summary: After the music-and-gymnastic stage, education restarts at a higher level: true knowledge is of universals, and the aim of education is the habit of abstraction, acquired through the mathematical sciences, which give ideas of relation and arouse thought. The commentator notes that in Plato's day mathematics was the mind's only instrument for reducing particulars to rule and order, though Plato already saw that geometrical forms are borrowed from the sensible world.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentator (introduction/analysis)

entries.label: Dialectic above mathematics
entries.summary: Ideas of number are secondary to a higher conception of knowledge: the dialectician stands above the mathematician as the mathematician above ordinary men, and the self-proving good is the truth to which all things ascend. The commentator presents the idea of good, viewed subjectively, as dialectic (division and collection, definition of essences, piercing hypotheses to the first principle) and says Plato's own dialogues exemplify this method; viewed objectively it is a power or cause aligning the outer and inner world of ideas.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentator (introduction/analysis)

entries.label: The good: vacant yet directive
entries.summary: The commentator calls the self-proving unity or idea of good 'a mere vision' admitting no distinct explanation, an abstraction comprehending no individuals (a vacancy Aristotle perceived but Plato did not), and argues the dialectical method advanced no further. Yet he adds that such vacant ideals can powerfully direct minds: a true ideal of what knowledge ought to be, unlike a false one such as the scholastic philosophy, presses inquiry forward toward unity, classification, and certainty.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentator (introduction/analysis)

entries.label: Education continued through life
entries.summary: The commentator credits Plato with holding that education continues through life and begins again in another, alongside his delight in the idea of good and solid geometry — but estimates this is the ideal life of the philosopher or genius, for the few, since worldly occupations crowd out study and most people lack the energy and the way to keep improving. He then lists practical counsels for self-education: choose an inclining subject, keep great authors as companions, give an hour a day to enquiry, judge by facts not opinion, and know one's own limits.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentator (introduction/analysis)

entries.label: Philosophers as kings
entries.summary: The speaker's 'third and greatest wave' of objection is the claim that cities and the human race will have no rest until philosophers rule or rulers do philosophy; defending it, he defines the philosopher as lover of the whole of wisdom rather than a part, and (with Glaucon pressing for precision) as lover of the vision of truth, unlike mere lovers of sights and sounds.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · Socrates and Glaucon

entries.label: Opposites two, each one
entries.summary: Because beauty and ugliness are opposites they are two; being two, each is one. The same holds of just/unjust, good/evil and every class: taken singly each is one, yet in combination with actions, things and each other they appear many.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · unnamed questioner proposing, unnamed interlocutor assenting

entries.label: Sight-lovers vs philosophers
entries.summary: Lovers of sounds and sights delight in fine tones, colours, forms and things made from them, but cannot see or love absolute beauty; the questioner contrasts them with those 'alone worthy of the name of philosophers'.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · unnamed questioner ('I replied')

entries.label: Dreamer vs wakeful knower
entries.summary: One who grasps beautiful things but not absolute beauty, or cannot follow a guide to it, likens dissimilar things and puts the copy in place of the real object: he dreams. One who distinguishes the idea from participating objects, placing neither where the other belongs, is wide awake.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · unnamed questioner and unnamed interlocutor

entries.label: Being pairs with knowing
entries.summary: What is known must be something that is; absolute being is (or may be) absolutely known and the utterly non-existent utterly unknown. Since knowledge corresponds to being and ignorance to not-being, anything that both is and is not needs a corresponding faculty between knowledge and ignorance.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · unnamed questioner with interlocutor's assent

entries.label: Faculties by sphere and result
entries.summary: Faculties are powers in us and other things (sight and hearing are examples). The questioner discerns them not by figure or colour but only by sphere and result: same sphere and result means the same faculty, a different sphere and result a different one.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · unnamed questioner proposing a method

entries.label: Particulars as riddles
entries.summary: The interlocutor compares particular beautiful, just and double/half things to a feast riddle and the children's puzzle of the eunuch and the bat: they have a double sense and cannot be fixed in the mind as being or not-being, both or neither.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · unnamed interlocutor ('he replied')

entries.label: Lovers of opinion named
entries.summary: Those who see only the many beautiful (or just) things and cannot follow a guide to the absolute are concluded to have opinion, not knowledge; the questioner proposes calling them lovers of opinion and calling those who love the truth in each thing lovers of wisdom. The interlocutor agrees the description is true and should not anger anyone.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK V · dialogue · unnamed questioner and unnamed interlocutor

entries.label: Who should rule the State?
entries.summary: Socrates next asks which of the two classes just distinguished—those who grasp the eternal and unchangeable, or those who wander among the many and variable—should rule, and proposes the test that whoever is best able to guard the State's laws and institutions should be guardians, with sight preferred to blindness.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Charge: philosophers useless
entries.summary: Adeimantus interposes that while no one can answer the argument step by step, experience shows the votaries of philosophy—pursued past youth—mostly become monsters or rogues, and the best of them useless to the world; he asks how cities can benefit from philosopher-rulers if philosophers are admittedly of no use to them.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Adeimantus

entries.label: Ship and mutineers parable
entries.summary: To plead the cause of the best men Socrates invents a figure of a ship whose captain is strong but dull of sight and barely knows navigation; the sailors who have never learned the art of steering fight for the helm, drug or chain the captain, and kill or throw overboard rivals, while the true pilot who attends to seasons, sky, stars and winds is denounced by them as a prater, star-gazer and good-for-nothing.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Uselessness: others' fault
entries.summary: Socrates says the accusers are right that the best philosophers seem useless, but the blame belongs to those who will not use them rather than to the philosophers themselves: the pilot need not beg sailors to be commanded, and the saying that the wise go to the doors of the rich is a lie—it is the one who wants governing that must go to the one able to govern.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Remnant retreats behind a wall
entries.summary: Of philosophy's worthy disciples only a small remnant survives; having tasted philosophy and seen the multitude's madness and the dishonesty of politicians, such a man will not join the wickedness around him, cannot resist it, and retires like a man sheltering behind a wall in a dust-storm to live out his own life and depart in peace—a great work, though not the greatest unless he finds a State suitable to him.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: No State fits philosophy
entries.summary: Socrates answers that not one of the governments now existing is suited to the philosophic nature, and that this is his accusation against them: like exotic seed in foreign soil the growth of philosophy degenerates and takes another character; only if philosophy finds in the State her own perfection would she be seen to be truly divine.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Living authority still needed
entries.summary: Socrates recalls that even their own constitution would always require some living authority holding the same idea of the constitution that guided its legislator in laying down the laws; the interlocutor confirms this was said earlier.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Socrates (first-person speaker, unnamed in the passage)

entries.label: Ordering philosophy safely
entries.summary: Socrates names the still-remaining problem: how the study of philosophy may be ordered so as not to be the ruin of the State, noting that great attempts carry risk and that the enquiry is not easy. He then declares he will argue that States should pursue philosophy not as now but in a different spirit.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Philosophy out of its season
entries.summary: Socrates describes present students of philosophy as beginning near childhood, giving it only time spared from moneymaking and housekeeping, and abandoning dialectic at its difficulty until in old age they go out like a sun that never relights. He prescribes the opposite course: studies suited to tender years, care of the body in youth, increasing exercise of the soul as intellect matures, and free ranging once civil and military duties are past.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Philosophers compelled to rule
entries.summary: Socrates argues that cities, States and individuals will never attain perfection until the small class of philosophers called useless but not corrupt are compelled to take care of the State and the State obeys them, or kings or their sons are divinely inspired with a love of true philosophy. Neither alternative is impossible, only difficult; he holds that this constitution has been, is, and will be whenever philosophy rules, and adds that one such man with one city obedient to his will would suffice.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Philosopher imitates fixed order
entries.summary: The mind set on true being attends to things fixed and immutable that move in rational order and neither injure nor are injured; through reverential converse with them the philosopher imitates and conforms to that order, becoming orderly and divine as human nature allows. If required to fashion himself and human nature in State or individual after what he beholds, he becomes a skilled artificer of justice, temperance and every civil virtue, working from a rubbed-clean tablet and looking between absolute justice, beauty and temperance and their human copy.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Socrates (addressing Adeimantus)

entries.label: Guardian must be a philosopher
entries.summary: Socrates now dares to say that the perfect guardian must be a philosopher, though such will be few because the required gifts rarely grow together: quick, high-spirited natures lack settled order and solid principle, while dependable natures are torpid over intellectual toil. Besides earlier trials in labours, dangers and pleasures, aspirants must be exercised in many kinds of knowledge to see whether the soul can endure the highest.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Good as cause of truth and being
entries.summary: Socrates names the idea of good the highest knowledge, without which any other knowledge or possession profits nothing. He then offers (as the good's offspring in the visible world) the sun, which is not sight but the author of sight: in like manner the good imparts truth to the known and the power of knowing to the knower, is above science and truth, and is the author of things' being and essence while itself exceeding essence in dignity and power.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Socrates (developing an analogy with Glaucon)

entries.label: Divided line of knowing
entries.summary: Socrates asks Glaucon to take a line cut into unequal parts for the visible and the intellectual and to divide each alike: in the visible, images (shadows, reflections) and then the animals and things made, the copy to the original as opinion to knowledge; in the intelligible, a lower stage in which the soul uses such figures as images and argues hypothetically (geometry and kindred sciences, with unexamined hypotheses) and a higher stage in which the soul rises above hypotheses to a first principle and proceeds through ideas alone.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Socrates (to Glaucon)

entries.label: Dialectic rises past hypotheses
entries.summary: Socrates says dialectic uses hypotheses not as first principles but as steps, ascending to the first principle of the whole and then descending through ideas to their consequences without reliance on sensible objects.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Geometry as understanding
entries.summary: Glaucon restates that the knowledge dialectic contemplates is clearer than the arts' hypothesis-bound notions, which are grasped by understanding rather than by sense or higher reason; he supposes Socrates would call geometry's habit understanding, intermediate between opinion and reason.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Glaucon

entries.label: Four faculties on a scale
entries.summary: Socrates posits four faculties of the soul corresponding to four divisions of objects: reason for the highest, understanding for the second, faith or conviction for the third, and perception of shadows for the last, graded by the truth-clearness of their respective objects.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Glaucon's assent
entries.summary: Glaucon replies that he understands and gives his assent, accepting Socrates' arrangement.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VI · dialogue · Glaucon

entries.label: Cave: shadows taken as truth
entries.summary: In Socrates' figure, people chained from childhood in an underground den see only the shadows of carried objects thrown on the wall, and their 'truth' is literally nothing but those shadows of images.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VII · dialogue · Socrates to Glaucon

entries.label: Release and ascent are painful
entries.summary: When a prisoner is released and turned toward the light, he suffers, still judges the shadows truer, and only accustoms himself gradually — shadows first, then reflections, then the sun itself.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VII · dialogue · Socrates to Glaucon

entries.label: Returner judged helpless, killed
entries.summary: The one who comes back down is dazzled, absurd at judging the shadows, and the prisoners would call ascent useless and would kill anyone caught loosing others and leading them up.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VII · dialogue · Socrates to Glaucon

entries.label: Allegory key: idea of good
entries.summary: Socrates appends the interpretation: the prison-house is the world of sight and the upward journey the soul's ascent into the intellectual world, where the idea of good appears last with effort and is, in his stated belief, the universal author of things beautiful and right and the source of reason and truth; he marks the opinion as uncertain and at Glaucon's request.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VII · dialogue · Socrates, with explicit qualification of the view as his own ('whether rightly or wrongly God knows')

entries.label: Philosophers must descend to rule
entries.summary: Socrates argues that guardians who reach the good must be compelled to descend again into the den and share its labours and honours; to Glaucon's objection that this is unjust, the legislator's aim answered is the happiness of the whole State rather than of one class, and such rulers are to rule from necessity rather than appetite for office.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VII · dialogue · Socrates; objection voiced by Glaucon

entries.label: Geometry aims at the eternal
entries.summary: Geometry matters only insofar as its higher, non-practical part eases the vision of the good and compels the soul toward full perfection of being; its real object is knowledge of the eternal, not of the transient, so it draws the soul toward truth.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VII · dialogue · Socrates, critiquing practising geometricians

entries.label: Order corrected: solid geometry
entries.summary: Socrates corrects the curriculum: after plane geometry should come solid geometry (cubes and depth), not solids in revolution; he attributes the branch's neglect to the absence of State patronage and of directors, though such studies would flourish under State encouragement.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VII · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Astronomy lifts soul (Glaucon)
entries.summary: Glaucon, revising his earlier praise at Socrates' rebuke, says astronomy compels the soul to look upwards and leads it from this world to another.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VII · dialogue · Glaucon

entries.label: Heavens as pattern, not truth
entries.summary: Socrates holds that the visible heaven, the fairest of visible things, is only a pattern: true motions, numbers and figures are apprehended by reason and not by sight, and a true astronomer will not look for exact truth in visible proportions.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VII · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Harmonics repeats sensory error
entries.summary: Socrates says harmony teachers, and the Pythagoreans likewise, labour over heard sounds and heard numbers only and never reach problems of natural harmony or why some numbers are harmonious and others not.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VII · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Studies as prelude to dialectic
entries.summary: Socrates holds that the studies have value for their object only when grasped in their mutual affinities, and that all of them are but the prelude to the strain to be learned, so that the skilled mathematician is not yet a dialectician.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VII · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Dialectic reaches first principle
entries.summary: Socrates names dialectic the intellect-only ascent by reason to the absolute good, and the one study that discards its hypotheses to reach a first principle, using the previously discussed sciences as handmaids and helpers.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VII · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Training sequence and late rule
entries.summary: Socrates prescribes a staged course: age should moderate the eristic misuse of argument; from thirty, five years of dialectic; then fifteen years of military and civic office as a test; and at fifty, chiefly contemplating the good while ruling in turn and training successors.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VII · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Absolute beauty and the One
entries.summary: The indexer gathers references to absolute beauty, good, justice, swiftness, temperance and unity (5.476–7.540), and contrasts 'the absolute and the many' (6.507), presenting these as one family of 'absolute' objects indexed from the dialogue.

entries.label: Editor on dialectic and eristic
entries.summary: A bracketed editor's note treats dialectic as the coping stone of knowledge, distinguished from eristic, and as employing scientific hypotheses as steps toward ideas and truth; the note concedes this conception was probably no clearer to Plato himself (referring to the Introduction), finds it firmer as analysis plus synthesis in Sophist and Statesman, and says the Laws demotes dialectic to question-and-answer discussion (7.820 C; 10.891).
entries.sourceLabel: Index and editorial apparatus · paratext · editorial commentator

entries.label: Editor on two-part education
entries.summary: A bracketed editor's note divides the Republic's education into (1) common Hellenic music and gymnastic — both ultimately for the soul, music (including literature) preceding gymnastic, shared by boys and girls, with fiction censored and fair surroundings essential — and (2) the rulers' special education: selection at twenty, ten years of arithmetic, geometry, astronomy and harmony pursued non-utilistically and combined through dialectic, five years of philosophy at thirty, fifteen years of public life, then philosophy again after fifty.
entries.sourceLabel: Index and editorial apparatus · paratext · editorial commentator

entries.label: Editorial: Idea of Good (Philebus)
entries.summary: Editorial note maintaining that the Idea of Good as named is an abstraction not otherwise found in Plato, probably akin to 'the true being of things', and that Plato never explained his meaning precisely. The editor suggests Plato valued abstractions above facts yet used the cave allegory to demand a firm starting point, and offers Philebus 65 A (Beauty, Symmetry, Truth) as the best insight into the ideal of perfection.
entries.sourceLabel: Index and editorial apparatus · paratext

entries.label: Tripartite and fourfold soul
entries.summary: Editorial essay describing the Republic's psychology as both continuous with and a development of the other dialogues: the division into reason, spirit and appetite here 'first assumes a precise form', underlies the classification of governments, and makes virtue the harmony of the elements (reason enforced by passion against appetite) and vice their anarchy. On the intellectual side the editor counts four faculties answering to four divisions of knowledge and the Platonic 'proportion', while judging these divisions 'partly real, partly formed by a logical process, which... has outrun fact' and pointing to the cave as illustration.
entries.sourceLabel: Index and editorial apparatus · paratext · editor (bracketed index commentary)

entries.summary: From sight to being: the philosopher, the ascent, and the idea of Good as the summit of education
entries.sourceLabel: Summary of source occurrences

entries.label: Five states, five souls
entries.summary: Resuming after the digression, the analysis recasts the scheme: besides the perfect State, Hellas has four noteworthy constitutions — Lacedaemonian/Cretan (timocratic), oligarchy, democracy, tyranny — with four matching individual natures. Working state first and then man will show whether the perfectly just or the tyrannical man is happier, and so settle whether Thrasymachus's argument or 'our own' is more convincing.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · unnamed analyst (dialogue reported)

entries.label: Muses' number splits the metals
entries.summary: In a jesting Muses' answer, the fall of the perfect State is traced to division among rulers caused by a fixed numerical law of human generation: rulers cannot reckon fertile seasons, marriages fail, 'inferior offspring' become rulers, gymnastic displaces music, and the gold/silver and iron/brass races mix and then pull apart over wealth, compromising on private property and enslaving their former fellow-citizens while keeping their warlike character. Timocracy, intermediate between aristocracy and oligarchy, results.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · unnamed analyst (Muses' answer quoted)

entries.label: Timocracy loses philosophy
entries.summary: Timocracy keeps the ideal's obedience to rulers, common meals and war/gymnastic training, but philosophy is corrupted, war arts prevail over peace arts, wealth is hoarded, and party spirit and ambition become its mark. The matching man is self-asserting, ill-educated yet fond of reading, obedient to rulers, hungry for honour won by arms, and later avaricious: shaped when his mother and the family servant reproach his retiring father, he settles at a middle point between them.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · unnamed analyst (Adeimantus's reply quoted)

entries.label: Oligarchy: two cities in one
entries.summary: Oligarchy arises when gold and silver possession makes riches outweigh virtue and lovers of money replace lovers of honour; political rights are confined by law to the rich. The city becomes two warring nations of rich and poor, guarded by no arms in the poor's hands, breeding drones with and without stings (paupers and rogues) through bad education and bad government. The matching man, frightened when he sees an honour-loving father ruined by informers, enthrones avarice: outwardly respectable, secretly slavish and mean, he hoards and fights with only a fraction of his resources.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · unnamed analyst (dialogue reported)

entries.label: Democracy: pleasing and lawless
entries.summary: Democracy takes power when the poor — reduced to dronage by usurers and extravagant habits encouraged by the rich — defeat them, kill or exile some, and give equal shares to all. Its life is freedom of speech and each doing what is right in his own eyes, so the city is 'not one but many', a bazaar where anything can be had: a pleasing, lawless, variety-loving government giving equality to equals and unequals alike and neglecting the training of statesmen. The matching man, son of a miserly oligarch, is lured by the drone's honey and wild companions into a battle in the soul that banishes modesty and temperance under renamed vices, then divides his time impartially between necessary and unnecessary pleasures, unable to rank any of them.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · unnamed analyst (dialogue reported)

entries.label: Tyrant-wolf devours the people
entries.summary: Tyranny grows out of democracy's exclusive love of freedom: anarchy spreads through the state and households until no citizen will bear any law. From the drones, rich and labouring classes the people raise a protector who, tasting human blood and bribing with debts and land, must 'become a wolf' — taking a bodyguard and standing as full-blown tyrant in the chariot of State. The people find they have nurtured a monster too strong to expel, beaten by the son they raised: liberty that ignores all order and reason passes into the worst servitude.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · unnamed analyst (dialogue reported)

entries.label: Symbol, not solution
entries.summary: The commentary accepts 216 but rejects Donaldson's mapping of the perfect number to the world and the imperfect to the state, his claim that the second harmony is a cube, and his gloss of 'two incommensurables' as 2 and 3 (reading instead two squares on irrational diameters of a side-5 figure). It closes the puzzle: solving the riddle would be useless, and Plato's real point is the symbolic contrast that a perfect or cyclical number presides over divine creation and an imperfect number over human generation, with numbers 5040 and 729 cited to gauge the problem's exactness.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Editorial commentary (editor/translator)

entries.label: Three pleasures ranked by knowledge
entries.summary: The second proof gives three kinds of pleasure answering to reason, passion, and desire, each nature praising only its own pleasures. The tie-break is experience and knowledge: only the philosopher has sampled the lower pleasures and can judge all three, while the money-maker and ambitious man judge by wealth or honour rather than reason; so rational pleasure is pleasantest, ambition's second, money-making's third.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates (dialogue), as paraphrased in the analysis

entries.label: True pleasure, not relief of pain
entries.summary: The third proof holds that many bodily pleasures are merely reliefs of pain or anticipations of relief and are misperceived (like a man halfway up mistaking the middle region for the top, or the grey for white against black), whereas some pleasures have no antecedent pains. Satisfaction of what has more being and truth (soul, the invariable) is truer than that of the mortal body; bodily pleasures are shadows mixed with contrast, and insatiable appetites leave a 'leaky' vessel (cf. Gorgias 243 A).
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates (dialogue), as paraphrased in the analysis

entries.label: King–tyrant gap: 729
entries.summary: The analysis calls the tyrannical man enslaved — the better part of his soul ruled by the worse, poorer and more miserable than any other, and worse still if he becomes a public tyrant — and then numbers the distance to the king: the tyrant's pleasure is a shadow of a shadow (third removed from the oligarch, the oligarch thrice removed from the king), 3×3 cubed = 729, the 'number of a beast' nearly equal to a year's 365×2 days and nights, making the king 729 times happier than the tyrant.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates (dialogue), as paraphrased in the analysis

entries.label: Soul as beast, lion, and man
entries.summary: Answering the claim that injustice pays if undetected, the analysis images the soul as a many-headed tame-and-wild beast, a lion, and a smaller man under one human skin: injustice feeds the beasts and starves the man, while justice strengthens the man and allies the lion to subdue the many-headed hydras. Vices map onto each element's misuse (intemperance looses the monster; sullenness fattens the lion; flattery turns it into a monkey), and education and law exist to install the ruling principle.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates (dialogue), as paraphrased in the analysis

entries.label: Editor on Book IX's pleasure theory
entries.summary: The commentary's closing introduction singles out three points of Book IX — the account of pleasure, the 729 interval, and the pattern in heaven — and judges the pleasure doctrine moderate: each soul-part should have its natural satisfaction, and pleasure is more than the absence of pain (cf. Philebus). Against the Cynics, towards the Epicureans, and since technicalised by Aristotle, it nevertheless rests on ancient illusions — treating a pleasure's transience as proof of unreality, and conflating the permanence of knowledge with a greater and longer-lasting pleasure.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Editorial commentary (editor/translator)

entries.label: 729: king to tyrant
entries.summary: The analyst reads the number 729 (the cube of 9, near the days and nights in a year) as Plato's formula for an immeasurable gap between the king and the tyrant, glossing it as one year of tyrannical life equaling about twelve hours of royal life; the steps to the cube are admittedly hard to reconstruct, the intermediate terms being counted as the side of a square.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · anonymous editor-analyst

entries.label: Plan: four bad constitutions
entries.summary: Glaucon recalls the digression's plan: from the true State and its man, four false constitutions and their four corresponding men were to be examined, so that by placing the most just beside the most unjust they could judge which life is happier and whether to follow Thrasymachus' advice on injustice or prefer justice. Socrates names the four distinct forms as Crete and Sparta (timocracy/oligarchy boundary is elsewhere called timocracy), oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny, tyranny being the fourth and worst disorder.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VIII · dialogue · Socrates and Glaucon

entries.label: Nuptial number and decline
entries.summary: In a mock solemn speech of the Muses, Socrates says even the best constitution must end: because human generation is governed by a number their 'intelligence alloyed with sense' cannot grasp, guardians breed out of season, the successors grow less cultivated (neglecting first music, then gymnastic), lose the art of telling gold, silver, brass and iron natures apart, and the mixing of metals produces dissimilarity, hatred and war. Editorial footnotes appended to the numerical passage give divergent computations and refer readers to the Introduction, so the arithmetic remains unsettled in this edition.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VIII · dialogue · Socrates, voicing the Muses (with Glaucon); footnotes by the editor

entries.label: Slight causes, deep stasis
entries.summary: The main speaker likens the State to a diseased body: where it is internally weak, a slight outside touch (oligarchical or democratical allies) or even no external provocation can set it warring with itself.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VIII · dialogue · Socrates ('I said')

entries.label: Democracy's violent birth
entries.summary: Democracy comes into being when the poor conquer their opponents, killing some and banishing some, give the rest equal freedom and power, and elect magistrates commonly by lot; the revolution may be by arms or by the opposite party's fear-driven withdrawal.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VIII · dialogue · Socrates, with respondent's agreement

entries.label: Democracy, embroidered robe
entries.summary: Because a man may say, do, and live as he likes, democracy yields the greatest variety of natures and is like an embroidered robe spangled with all flowers — pleasing to many, a bazaar of constitutions for a founder, and a dispensing of equality to equals and unequals alike.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VIII · dialogue · Socrates ('I said')

entries.label: Necessary vs. unnecessary pleasures
entries.summary: Necessary pleasures cannot be got rid of and their satisfaction benefits us (e.g., plain eating for health and life); unnecessary pleasures can be trained away and harm body and soul — the drone is slave to these, the oligarch subject only to the necessary.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VIII · dialogue · Socrates ('I said')

entries.label: Oligarchic youth turns democratic
entries.summary: A youth miserly raised, tasting drones' honey and meeting purveyors of refined pleasures, is changed by desires from without aiding akin desires within; aided by father's counsel, the oligarchical part fights back in faction, but false conceits seize the soul's citadel, expelling modesty and temperance under renamed vices and ushering in anarchy and waste as liberty and magnificence.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VIII · dialogue · Socrates ('I said')

entries.label: Democratic man's daily anarchy
entries.summary: Balancing pleasures in a day-to-day equilibrium, the democratic man admits no advice distinguishing good from bad desires, swings from drink to diet to gymnastics to philosophy to politics to war or business, calls this lawless life joy and freedom, and is an epitome of many lives answering to the spangled state.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VIII · dialogue · Socrates ('I said')

entries.label: Liberty flips into slavery
entries.summary: Democracy's own good, freedom, is pursued insatiably to its ruin; the excessive increase of anything reacts in the opposite direction, so the same disease magnified by liberty overmasters democracy and the greatest tyranny and slavery arise from the most extreme liberty.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK VIII · dialogue · Socrates ('I said')

entries.label: Making of the tyrannical man
entries.summary: Socrates recounts how the democratic man's son is drawn into a lawless life his seducers call 'perfect liberty'; when the 'tyrant-makers' lose hold, they implant a master passion — imaged as a monstrous winged drone — to lord over his idle lusts. Nourished by his other lusts, this ruler breaks out with Madness as captain of the guard, extinguishing remaining shame and good opinions and purging temperance. On this account Love is rightly called a tyrant; drunkenness and derangement show the same spirit, and the tyrannical man arises when nature or habit makes him drunken, lustful, passionate. (A footnote glosses 'good opinions' as opinions or appetites 'such as are deemed to be good'.)
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IX · dialogue · Socrates (interlocutor: Adeimantus)

entries.label: Soul–State parallel
entries.summary: Socrates asserts a standing parallel: as man is to man in virtue and happiness, so State is to State — each character in the individual matches a constitution. Applied to the tyrant, the tyrannical city is enslaved and degraded, and likewise his soul is full of meanness, its best elements enslaved while a small ruling part, the worst and maddest, commands; such a soul is a slave's soul, incapable of acting voluntarily or doing what it desires, poor, insatiable and fearful.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IX · dialogue · Socrates (interlocutor now identified as Glaucon)

entries.label: True versus apparent pleasure
entries.summary: The third trial (said to be whispered by 'a sage', first reported by Socrates) claims that only the wise person's pleasure is true and pure, the rest shadows. Socrates elicits that pleasure and pain are motions with a neutral state between them; people call rest after pain or pain after pleasure by the opposite name, though the neutral state cannot be both — so reliefs of pain only appear pleasurable. Pleasures of smell are given as pure pleasures without antecedent or ensuing pain; the upper/middle/lower region analogy shows how the ignorant, never seeing the true upper region, misjudge their position by contrast alone.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IX · dialogue · Socrates (reporting a unnamed 'sage'; questioning Glaucon)

entries.label: Pleasure misread by ignorance
entries.summary: Socrates argues that people inexperienced in the truth mistake pain, the relief of pain, and a neutral state for real pleasure, because they contrast pain with absence of pain rather than with true pleasure.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IX · dialogue · Socrates (questioning)

entries.label: Being grades true pleasure
entries.summary: Through Socrates' questioning, the interlocutor concedes that bodily satisfactions have less truth and essence than those of soul, so what is filled with more real being enjoys more true and abiding pleasure, while lesser being yields an illusory pleasure.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IX · dialogue · Socrates, with respondent's assent

entries.label: Lives of shadow pleasure
entries.summary: Socrates depicts those ignorant of wisdom and virtue as grazing between pain and satiety like cattle and fighting over insubstantial fillings; their pleasures, being shadow-pictures coloured by contrast, incite insane desires, as with the Greeks fighting over Helen's phantom.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IX · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Reason-guided truest pleasures
entries.summary: Socrates asserts that money- and honour-lovers who pursue their proper pleasures under reason and knowledge attain the truest pleasures available to their nature, and that when the whole soul follows the philosophical principle each part does its own work and enjoys its best pleasure; the further a part is from reason, the more illusive its pleasure.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IX · dialogue · Socrates, with respondent's assent

entries.label: Tyrant 729 times from king
entries.summary: Socrates proposes one genuine and two spurious pleasures and places the tyrant three remove from the oligarch and the oligarch three from the royal type, so that in the completed solid calculation the king lives 729 times more pleasantly than the tyrant — a number relevant to human life per the dialogue, with an editorial footnote noting 729 nearly equals the year's days and nights.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IX · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Triple-animal soul image
entries.summary: Socrates has Glaucon model a many-headed beast, a lion, and a man joined into one outer human form, and uses it against the claim that injustice profits: injustice feeds monster and lion while starving the inner man, whereas justice lets the inner man govern, cultivating the gentle heads and making the lion an ally that unites the parts.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IX · dialogue · Socrates (directing the modeling)

entries.label: Rule by the best element
entries.summary: Socrates answers that each person should serve the best, in whom the Divine rules — as Thrasymachus wrongly denied is harmful — or failing that be governed by an external authority; this is also the purpose of law and of the authority over children that installs a ruling guardian element in them.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IX · dialogue · Socrates, with respondent's assent

entries.label: Inner city and heavenly pattern
entries.summary: For Socrates the understanding man shapes studies and bodily habit toward the soul's harmony rather than health or beauty, regulates wealth by the needs of the city within him, and accepts only ennobling honours; he rules the ideal city patterned on one in heaven — whose actual existence is left open — which he may behold and by which he orders his own life and house.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK IX · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Constitutional forms and decline
entries.summary: The entry distinguishes the ideal aristocracy sketched in book 4 (8.544 E–545 D) from 'aristocracy' in the ordinary sense (1.338 D) and lists defective constitutions: timocracy or 'Spartan polity', oligarchy, democracy, tyranny, cross-referencing Government and State.
entries.sourceLabel: Index and editorial apparatus · paratext · index compiler

entries.label: Editorial: constitutions compared
entries.summary: Editorial note arguing that the Republic's classification of constitutions (king/one best man, aristocracy, then timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, tyranny, each tied to divisions of the soul) differs from the Statesman's law-based division and the Laws' 'two mother forms' of monarchy and democracy; it adds that Aristotle reproduces much of this but coins a middle-class polity. A companion index entry lists the four imperfect forms and the succession of changes in states.
entries.sourceLabel: Index and editorial apparatus · paratext

entries.label: Decline of regimes into tyranny
entries.summary: The index entries 'Timocracy', 'Tyranny', and 'Tyrant, the' sketch a descent: timocracy's origin in Republic 8. 545 foll., tyranny as injustice on the grand scale and the wretchedest government, the tyrant's rise, taxes, army, purgation of the city, his misery, lack of friends or real pleasure, and his posthumous punishment.

entries.label: Pattern in heaven
entries.summary: Near the close of Republic IX the heavenly pattern replaces the city of philosophers on earth: the vision is now distant, yet also the rule of man's life within the individual, striking a note that prepares for the revealed future life of the following Book while keeping the political ideal realizable in the individual.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · anonymous editor-analyst

entries.label: Imitation thrice removed
entries.summary: In the paraphrased Book X, God makes the one bed of nature and the carpenter a second bed, while the painter imitates the carpenter's bed and so is thrice removed from truth, catching only one appearance of a thing; set beside the arts of use and making, imitation has neither science nor true opinion, being only play or sport.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates, voiced in the analyst's paraphrase (Glaucon replying)

entries.label: Poetry vs the better soul
entries.summary: Since the same object appears differently at different distances or media and only measure and calculation settle the conflict, imitation is allied to the worse faculty and chiefly displays the sorrowful, irrational part of the soul, while reason is not easily displayed to a mixed crowd; the poet therefore paints inferior truth and an inferior part of the soul and is refused authority over the mind.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates, voiced in the analyst's paraphrase (Glaucon replying)

entries.label: Poetry's ban and her apology
entries.summary: Because poetry feeds grief and coarse merriment until they rule at home, all of it except hymns to the gods and praises of famous men is prohibited, with law and reason rather than pleasure and pain to rule; yet poetry is offered an apology and readmission on condition of proving itself useful as well as delightful, against the acknowledged ancient quarrel between poetry and philosophy and with the soul's good or evil as the stake.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates, voiced in the analyst's paraphrase; interlocutor agrees

entries.label: Soul's indestructibility
entries.summary: Each thing is destroyed only by its own inherent evil; injustice, the soul's proper corruption, does not kill the soul (or criminals would die unaided), and bodily evil cannot destroy what is a different thing — so the soul is immortal and everlasting, of the fairest and simplest composition, seen at present encrusted like the sea-god Glaucus and best viewed in philosophy.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · Socrates, voiced in the analyst's paraphrase (interlocutor objecting and conceding)

entries.label: Art feeds passion, not reason
entries.summary: The commentator reports Plato's Tenth Book charge that imitation expresses the emotional rather than the rational part of us and, refusing the Aristotelian purgation of passions, only lets us indulge them; but the commentator grants that voiced feeling can sometimes console and heal what is pent up.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Sense-poetry vs idea-philosophy
entries.summary: Explains the ancient quarrel by allying poetry with particulars of sense and philosophy (Socrates and Plato) with universals and abstraction, noting that Aristotle reverses the valuation by finding poetry, unlike history, concerned with universals (Poetics c. 9, 3).
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Poetry in the service of tyranny
entries.summary: A further count in the indictment: poets, with sophists and rhetoricians, are cast as false teachers and courtiers of tyrants, and the commentator asserts that despotism cannot be maintained without corrupted literature and claims on the imagination of the masses.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Art joins thought and feeling
entries.summary: Against eradication of the emotions, the commentator holds emotions are neither good nor bad in themselves: art presents thought in the form of feeling and, as a necessary compromise of ideal and exact, stands between sense and ideas; since imagination underlies thought and language, banishing it would be impossible as well as suicidal.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Poetry that serves mankind
entries.summary: Reading the banishment of the poets as protest against degenerate verse rather than literal exile, the commentator imagines a poetry of divine truth and justice, measures named poets by that standard (with praise for some and fault found with others, including that one 'has left no way of life'), and closes with the question of how the gift of poesy may be devoted to the good of mankind.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Choice within necessity
entries.summary: In the analysis of the Myth of Er, chance in the order of lots may be overcome by choosing with wisdom; hibitual goodness is inferior and must add knowledge to act well in new circumstances (the Coleridge parallel is the commentator's), and free will to reject evil is real though bounded by necessity and unequal circumstances.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Ancients lacked idea of progress
entries.summary: The commentator observes that Plato and Aristotle seem hardly ever to have considered the regular growth or progress of states and institutions: ancient fixation on divinely sanctioned fundamental law, he suggests, helps explain Plato's intolerance of innovators (though Plato allowed studied foreign improvements and some change short of altering fundamental institutions). Experience gave the Greeks cycles of civilization rather than growth; the idea of progress and of a philosophy of history is modern, fed by Rome, the Church, revolutions, material prosperity, and the study of history, while the small Greek state's vision was 'necessarily limited'.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentator (introduction/analysis)

entries.label: Ideal republics after Plato
entries.summary: The commentator claims that writers after Plato likewise used an 'ideal Republic' to carry thoughts they could not express definitely or that outran their age. The nearest classical parallel is Cicero's De Republica, which imitates the Republic's portraits, democracy, tyrant and vision of Er (romanized as the Somnium Scipionis) but falls short in dramatic art and originality while sounding the note of Roman patriotism.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentator (introduction/analysis)

entries.label: Cicero romanizes Plato
entries.summary: The commentary judges Cicero's De Republica a Roman imitation of Plato: the Somnium Scipionis 'romanizes' Er's vision and adds an immortality argument derived from the Phaedrus, yet remains an inferior dream; the dialogues make speeches rather than converse, and the philosophical writings show no original thinker.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Augustine's City of God
entries.summary: St Augustine's De Civitate Dei, prompted by the fall of Rome as Plato's Republic by the decline of Greek politics, answers the pagan claim that Christianity ruined the empire by blaming pagan vice, tracing sacred and profane history toward a true City of God. The commentary finds the work polemical and wholly uncritical in its use of sources, yet holding passages 'for all time'.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Dante's De Monarchia
entries.summary: Dante's De Monarchia presents a universal empire, divinely authorized yet distinct from the Papacy and justified by Roman virtue; its case mixes a priori reasoning with misused Scripture, history, and Aristotle, but is anchored in the misery of the world and the hope that life may pass 'in freedom and peace'. The commentary stresses the vision is inseparable from Dante's own age and beliefs.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: More's Utopia mirrors England
entries.summary: More, writing at about 34-35, brings 'the light of Plato' to bear on post-Wars-of-the-Roses England, placing Book One's clerical corruption, luxury, poverty, and war beside the ideal commonwealth of Book Two built with Plato's help and committed to community of property.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: More's feigned travel narrative
entries.summary: The commentary credits More's dramatic invention and art of feigning as a Platonic disciple's: he builds on lines of Vespucci, mixes real figures (John Clement, Peter Giles) with the imaginary Hythloday, adds pseudo-documentary disputes and excuses so that the island's location is 'lost with him' and Utopia remains unknown.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Utopia's tolerance, veiled author
entries.summary: The Utopians exclude unbelievers from office but punish no unbelief and use non-sectarian prayer, which the commentary reads as More exceeding both Plato and his age in tolerance (with a footnote where dissenters are exiled as seditious, not irreligious). Yet More disclaims agreement with all Utopian customs, so the commentary urges keeping the veil over his own voice.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Ideals and the Idea of Good
entries.summary: The closing sections (VII-VIII) argue that ideals, like the examples of great men, raise individuals and states though never directly practicable, remaining 'visions of a world unrealized' with which Plato fixes the mind's eye in the distance. They set beside each other the modern hopes of mankind's future in this world and of individual life beyond it, warn that language's figures must not enslave meditation on God, and name Christ as the human image of that Idea of Good Plato 'saw dimly in the distance'.
entries.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

entries.label: Ban on imitative poetry
entries.summary: The speaker says the rule excluding imitative poetry is vindicated now that the parts of the soul are distinguished, and asserts that poetical imitations ruin the hearers' understanding unless one knows their true nature.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK X · dialogue · Socrates (per dialogue attribution)

entries.label: One form, many artifacts
entries.summary: Where many things share a name there is one idea or form; many beds and tables exist but only one form of each, and craftsmen make particular artifacts in accord with the form without making the forms themselves.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK X · dialogue · Socrates (per dialogue attribution)

entries.label: Mirror makes appearances
entries.summary: A spun mirror can produce everything at once, but only appearances; the painter is likewise a creator of appearances rather than real things.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK X · dialogue · Socrates and unnamed interlocutor

entries.label: Three beds, third from truth
entries.summary: Three beds and three makers are distinguished: the natural bed made by God (one only), the carpenter's particular bed, and the painter's work; the imitator stands third in descent from nature, and the tragic poet is thrice removed from truth.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK X · dialogue · Socrates and unnamed interlocutor

entries.label: Poets copy images only
entries.summary: Painting imitates things as they appear, and the imitator who lightly touches a small image can deceive the ignorant; poets likewise copy images of virtue without reaching the truth. Asked what State Homer governed, war he won, invention he made, or school he founded, the interlocutor answers 'no', so the poets lack genuine knowledge of their subjects.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK X · dialogue · Socrates, with Glaucon replying

entries.label: Using, making, imitating
entries.summary: Three arts attend to any thing: using, making, imitating. Correctness is relative to use, so the user has knowledge and instructs the maker, who has only correct belief (e.g. flute-player over flute-maker), while the imitator has neither knowledge nor right opinion of the goodness of his copies and so depicts what appears good to the ignorant crowd.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK X · dialogue · Socrates and unnamed interlocutor

entries.label: Poetry feeds the passions
entries.summary: Hearing others' lamentations loosens the pity we restrain in our own losses and strengthens sorrow at home (comedy likewise feeds buffoonery); poetry generally feeds and waters lust, anger, pleasure and pain instead of drying them up, harming even the best of us, who would be ashamed to act as we happily watch depicted.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK X · dialogue · Socrates and unnamed interlocutor

entries.label: Exile, with chance of return
entries.summary: Only hymns to the gods and praises of famous men may remain in the state, lest pleasure and pain rule; yet the quarrel of philosophy and poetry is acknowledged, and poetry or its prose defenders may plead that it is useful as well as pleasant. Until such a defence succeeds, the hearer of this argument is to guard the city within him against poetry's seductions.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK X · dialogue · Socrates and Glaucon

entries.label: Own evil destroys each thing
entries.summary: Socrates proposes that the corrupting element is the evil and the saving element the good, and that each thing (eyes, corn, timber, metal) has an inherent evil which, if anything destroys it, is what destroys it; good or what is neither good nor evil will not.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK X · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Soul's vices do not dissolve it
entries.summary: Socrates asks whether the soul's own evils — injustice, intemperance, cowardice, ignorance — waste and consume the soul as bodily disease wastes the body; Glaucon agrees they do not bring the soul to death and separate it from the body.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK X · dialogue · Socrates (question) and Glaucon (assent)

entries.label: External harm cannot kill soul
entries.summary: Using the example that bad food destroys the body only by producing the body's own disease, Socrates argues that merely external evil cannot dissolve the soul unless it engenders an evil of the soul; hence fever, the knife, or dismemberment cannot destroy the soul unless the person becomes more unjust thereby.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK X · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Soul is immortal
entries.summary: Socrates concludes that a soul indestructible by inherent or external evil must exist forever, and so is immortal; from this he infers the souls are always the same in number, neither increasing nor diminishing, and are of one fairest nature rather than a variegated compound.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK X · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Seeing the soul as it is
entries.summary: Socrates tells Glaucon that the soul as presently seen is marred by communion with the body, like the sea-god Glaucus encrusted and broken, so its true image must be sought through its love of wisdom and kinship with the eternal, freed from the growths of earthly life.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK X · dialogue · Socrates

entries.label: Myth of Er: judgement
entries.summary: Socrates, reporting Er the Pamphylian who returned to life, describes souls judged at the openings of heaven and earth carrying the marks of their deeds, a thousand-year journey, punishment and reward tenfold for every wrong or good deed, and the doomed Ardiaeus prevented from escaping the cavern and carried off to hell.
entries.sourceLabel: BOOK X · dialogue · Socrates (reporting Er)

entries.label: The case against poetry
entries.summary: Editorial essay presenting the Republic as Plato's first serious examination of poetry's place in education and the state. It traces a two-stage argument: in Books II–III the epic and tragic tales are tested for truth and fitness, and objectionable passages are to be expunged under censorship; in Book X the charge deepens — the poet is an impostor thrice removed from truth whose imitations supply corrupt models — ending in banishment unless 'the lovers of poetry' answer the charges. The essay sets this beside the Laws, where the poet is tolerated only in harmony with the laws.
entries.sourceLabel: Index and editorial apparatus · paratext · editor (bracketed index commentary)

entries.label: Immortality and Er's myth
entries.summary: Editorial claims that pre-existence and immortality are assumed rather than proved here (recollection being at most glanced at in Er's water of Unmindfulness), and that the immortality argument is 'chiefly of a verbal character' and less emphatic than the Phaedo's. It reads Er's narrative as the favoured mythic vehicle for rewards, punishments and the choice of lives, with the philosopher's wisdom securing a good choice rather than release from embodiment, and suggests the transmigration doctrine came via Pythagorean channels from an Oriental source but 'probably had a real hold on his mind'.
